Aki and I played around with some of these ideas when writing the Waic paper; maybe we should come back to it. A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
messages.body_plain:
Bob: yes, I see what I was missing now... thanks!
Matt: what you've written makes complete sense to me... but...

Unfortunately, the implementations of CGS available in r packages (lda and topicmodels) seem to fall rather short of my needs. I'm a researcher, so uncertainty matters to me because producing just a point estimate wouldn't be acceptable for publication (for good reason, IMHO). It looks like I could "hack" either of those packages to call them repeatedly but the mixing across such iterations may just be so poor that NUTS would be faster. More importantly, neither lda or topicmodels is designed to accommodate prior information on how the word distribution differs across topics -- both have just a single parameter for beta (as well as alpha) but my prior knowledge is in how beta differs across topics. Recall that this was my strategy for navigating the multi-modality problems that Bob mentioned (I should be able to keep increasing the strength of my priors until the posterior becomes unimodal). To give you more specific detail on my particular problem: my purpose is to estimate the share of each topic discussed in each of 50 documents. I have 50 to 100 pre-determined topics (they are industry names taken from NAICS codes, such as "Oil and Gas Extraction") to which I add an additional topic I call "misc" for none of the above. From these topic descriptions, I have constructed my 1000 to 4000 word vocabulary (e.g. it contains "oil", "gas", "extraction", "oil extraction", and "gas extractrion"). In setting the prior on beta, I can make it so that the word "oil" is more probable than other words when the topic is "oil and gas extraction" (I might have to experiment with how strong it needs to be to ensure that the term "oil" is most associated with "oil and gas extraction", which is what I meant by making the posterior unimodal). So, unless there is some way to rehabilitate the lda and/or topicmodels packages, calling stan from r appears to be my only hope short of a radical departure from the comfort of my r platform... well, unless there is some model other than LDA that would be more appropriate here (as an economist, I'm somewhat new to topic models and LDA seemed to be sufficiently appropriate and accepted as a standard approach but I would certainly welcome a better suggestion). Unfortunately, after letting my machine crunch overnight (approximately 12 hours), stan had made 0 progress on my problem (still on the first iteration). Here's my stan code (which is slightly modified, from the version in manual that Bob and I discussed, to accommodate a different prior on beta for each topic):

data{
  int <lower = 2> T;                // Num Topics
  int <lower = 2> V;                // Num Words in Vocabulary
  int <lower = 1> M;                // Num Docs
  int <lower = 0> K[V,M];           // search term counts in each of the M docs
  vector <lower = 0> [T] alpha[M];  // topic prior
  vector <lower = 0> [V] beta[T];   // word prior
}
parameters{
  simplex [T] theta[M]; // topic distribution for each of the M docs
  simplex [V] phi[T]; // word distribution for each of the T topics

}
model{
  for (m in 1:M)

    theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha[m]);  //prior
  for (t in 1:T)
    phi[t] ~ dirichlet(beta[t]);     //prior
  for (v in 1:V) {
    for (m in 1:M) {
      real gamma [T];
      for (t in 1:T)
        gamma[t] <- log(theta[m,t]) + log(phi[t,v]); //likelihood
      increment_log_prob(K[v,m]*log_sum_exp(gamma));
    }
  }
}

Here's my r code that calls stan:

library(rstan)
library(reshape2)

##### Import data files
Search.Term.Counts <- read.csv("string_title_year_count.csv")
Industry.Terms <- read.csv("search_terms_and_industries.csv")

# data cleaning: restrict to year 2012 and remove a few negative counts (probably due to a coding mistake upstream)
Search.Term.Counts.t <- subset(Search.Term.Counts,year==2012)
Search.Term.Counts.t$count <- ifelse(Search.Term.Counts.t$count < 0, 0, Search.Term.Counts.t$count)

# extract Num.Words.In.Vocabulary and Num.Docs from Search.Term.Counts
Num.Words.In.Vocabulary <- length(levels(Search.Term.Counts.t$string))
Num.Docs <- length(levels(as.factor(Search.Term.Counts.t$title)))

# extract Num.Topics [= Num.Industries + 1] from Industry.Terms
Num.Topics <- length(levels(as.factor(Industry.Terms$code)))+1

# extract Search.Term.Counts
melted.Search.Term.Counts <- melt(Search.Term.Counts.t[,c("title","string","count")], id=c("title", "string"))
Search.Term.Counts.Array <- acast(melted.Search.Term.Counts, string ~ title)

# Create the simply flat topic prior
# alpha here represents the virtual count of times we've seen this topic for this doc (akin to the beta distribution's parameters so that 1 is a flat uniform)
# Steyvers n Griffiths (2007) suggest 50/T, which is actually around 1 here anyway
Topic.Prior <- matrix(1,nrow=Num.Topics, ncol=Num.Docs)
rownames(Topic.Prior) <- c(levels(as.factor(Industry.Terms$code)),"000")
colnames(Topic.Prior) <- levels(as.factor(Search.Term.Counts.t$title))

# Create the topic prior which is flat but to which I'll add additional weight allocated for search terms known to be associated with particular industries
# beta here represents the virtual count of times we've seen this word used in this topic
# Steyvers n Griffiths (2007) suggest 0.01, which is improper, but they acknowledge that it should depend on vocabulary, num docs, etc... so I'll stick with 1 that corresponds to a flat uniform
Word.Prior <- matrix(1,nrow=Num.Words.In.Vocabulary, ncol=Num.Topics)
rownames(Word.Prior) <- levels(Search.Term.Counts.t$string)
colnames(Word.Prior) <- c(levels(as.factor(Industry.Terms$code)),"000")

# add information to the word prior
# loop thru each industry (not including the misc topic category)
# find the maximum number of words in that industry's search terms
# loop thru that industry's search terms to appropriately increment the prior for cases of individual terms in a search string of multiple words:
# the individual word should be more associated with misc and the whole search string of multiple words should be more associated with the industry
for (Current.Industry.Index in 1:(ncol(Word.Prior)-1)) {
  Industry.Code <- colnames(Word.Prior)[Current.Industry.Index]
  Current.Industry.Terms <- subset(Industry.Terms,code == Industry.Code)
  Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms <- sapply(gregexpr("\\W+", Current.Industry.Terms$string), function(x) sum(x>0) ) + 1
  Max.Num.Terms <- max(Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms)
  for (Current.String.Index in 1:nrow(Current.Industry.Terms)) {
    if (as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]) %in% rownames(Word.Prior)) {
      Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),Industry.Code] <- Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),Industry.Code] + Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms[Current.String.Index]
      Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),"000"] <- Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),"000"] + (Max.Num.Terms - Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms[Current.String.Index])
    }
  }
}

##########################################################################################
# Analyze with Stan
##########################################################################################

# reshaping the data as required by Stan -- packed into a list: counts as a VxM array, topic prior as a TxM array, and word prior as a VxM array
StanInputData <- list(T = Num.Topics, V = Num.Words.In.Vocabulary, M = Num.Docs, K = Search.Term.Counts.Array, alpha = t(Topic.Prior), beta = t(Word.Prior))

# run stan on the file, compile to C [stanc()], and iteratively draw samples from the posterior [sampling()]
stan.fit <- stan(file="LDA.stan", data=StanInputData, seed = 12345, iter=1000, chains=4)

On Thu, Aug 28, 2014 at 10:22 PM, Matt Hoffman <mdho...@cs.princeton.edu> wrote:

> Stan can be used to fit LDA. But you may be disappointed if you compare its ability to find good parameters quickly with a standard collapsed Gibbs sampler.
>
> CGS is a really surprisingly good stochastic search algorithm for LDA—it seems to be much easier to optimize the log-likelihood in "z-space" (the word-topic assignments) than in "theta-phi-space" (the topics and topic weights). One reason is sparsity—if you use Dirichlet priors with small hyperparameters and sum out the z variables (which you need to in Stan), then you wind up with a highly nonconvex sparsity-inducing prior. Gradient-based optimization on these kinds of nonconvex problems is very, very hard, and since NUTS relies very heavily on the use of gradient information to tell it where to explore, it's challenging for it to figure out what topics should be active in what documents. (Although in principle it'll figure it out eventually.)
>
> What NUTS is good at is mixing quickly and delivering large numbers of effectively independent samples. Nobody really knows what the mixing speed of CGS is like, and most people don't care—for most topic modeling applications people aren't really interested in quantifying the uncertainty in their parameter estimates.
>
> Matt
>

messages.body_plain:
1.  Rather than this:

  for(j in 1:J) {
      for(t in 1:T)
            lambda[t,j] ~ gamma(nu[j]/2,nu[j]/2) ;

you can use:

  for (t in 1:T)

    lambda[t] ~ gamma(nu / 2, nu / 2);

Even better would be to not divide nu by 2 twice, but to do it once
and assign it to a temporary.

2.   Replace

    for (t in 1:T) {

        for (j in 1:J)
            lambdainvsqrt[t][j] <- inv_sqrt(lambda[t][j]) ;
        LSigma[t] <- LRho * diag_matrix(sigma) * diag_matrix(lambdainvsqrt[t]) ;
    }

with

   {
      matrix[J,J] LRho_times_diag_matrix_sigma;
      LRho_sigma <- diag_post_multiply(LRho, sigma);

      for (t in 1:T) {

        for (j in 1:J)
            lambdainvsqrt[t][j] <- inv_sqrt(lambda[t][j]) ;
        LSigma[t] <- diag_post_multiply(LRho_sigma, lambda_inv_sqrt[t]);
    }

It may be even faster in a loop due to the sparsity.  In just
two dimensions, you can just write

  LSigma[t,1,1] <- ...
  LSigma[t,2,2] <- ...
  LSigma[t,2,1] <- ...
  LSigma[t,1,2] <- 0;  // lower triangular

with ... replaced by the reuslt of all the above matrix multiplication.
Make sure to save intermediate computations.

3.  If you don't need to save lambda_inv_sqrt[t], make it a local in the
same scope.

4.  This isn't a speed issue per se, but Andrew's been very down on the constrained
uniform priors (though we still have some in our manual):

    vector<lower=0,upper=100>[J] sigma ;    // scale of multivariate vector

    vector<lower=2,upper=30>[J] nu ;        // degrees of freedom of multivariate vector

Rather than this, you can just put a real prior on sigma and nu and leave
them unconstrained (well, they need lower=0 at least).

5.  Given that you only have a two-dimensional Cholesky factor, you could
just parameterize directly on the correlation rho.

- Bob

On Aug 31, 2014, at 11:09 PM, Bentley Coffey <bentley...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> Unfortunately, the implementations of CGS available in r packages (lda and topicmodels) seem to fall rather short of my needs. I'm a researcher, so uncertainty matters to me because producing just a point estimate wouldn't be acceptable for publication (for good reason, IMHO).

Using LDA for anything other than exploratory data analysis
seems dangerous.  What do you think the uncertainty is going
to be characterizing that isn't highly dependent on your prior
strength in this case?

> It looks like I could "hack" either of those packages to call them repeatedly but the mixing across such iterations may just be so poor that NUTS would be faster.

It's pretty much hopeless trying to mix the multiple modes of LDA.

> More importantly, neither lda or topicmodels is designed to accommodate prior information on how the word distribution differs across topics -- both have just a single parameter for beta (as well as alpha) but my prior knowledge is in how beta differs across topics. Recall that this was my strategy for navigating the multi-modality problems that Bob mentioned (I should be able to keep increasing the strength of my priors until the posterior becomes unimodal).

It still won't be convex, but with enough prior strength
you can push down the modes you don't want.  You still probably
won't get proper exploration of the posterior.

> To give you more specific detail on my particular problem: my purpose is to estimate the share of each topic discussed in each of 50 documents. I have 50 to 100 pre-determined topics (they are industry names taken from NAICS codes, such as "Oil and Gas Extraction") to which I add an additional topic I call "misc" for none of the above. From these topic descriptions, I have constructed my 1000 to 4000 word vocabulary (e.g. it contains "oil", "gas", "extraction", "oil extraction", and "gas extractrion"). In setting the prior on beta, I can make it so that the word "oil" is more probable than other words when the topic is "oil and gas extraction" (I might have to experiment with how strong it needs to be to ensure that the term "oil" is most associated with "oil and gas extraction", which is what I meant by making the posterior unimodal).

> So, unless there is some way to rehabilitate the lda and/or topicmodels packages, calling stan from r appears to be my only hope short of a radical departure from the comfort of my r platform... well, unless there is some model other than LDA that would be more appropriate here (as an economist, I'm somewhat new to topic models and LDA seemed to be sufficiently appropriate and accepted as a standard approach but I would certainly welcome a better suggestion).

It depends what you're trying to do.  If you are assuming each document
is made up out of several topics, then LDA's a reasonable model.

But you have to be careful with the prior on the document topic proportions
(theta in your model and the original LDA papers).  The strength of that prior
will determine how many topics get non-negligible probability in a document,
and this in turn plays off against the topic distributions themselves.

> Unfortunately, after letting my machine crunch overnight (approximately 12 hours), stan had made 0 progress on my problem (still on the first iteration).

Do you know if you ran out of memory?  I'd think this would be slow,
but not 12 hours per iteration slow.

Given your strong priors, you could try initializing theta and phi

>     }

You might be able to define a collapsed Gibbs sampler for your
model in JAGS.  Or just write the Gibbs sampler in R directly --- it's
a pretty easy one.

> Here's my r code that calls stan:

I don't speak R well enough to get through the rest.

> library(rstan)

> ##### Import data files

> Num.Docs <- length(levels(as.factor(Search.Term.Counts.t$title)))
>
> # extract Num.Topics [= Num.Industries + 1] from Industry.Terms
> Num.Topics <- length(levels(as.factor(Industry.Terms$code)))+1
>
> # extract Search.Term.Counts
> melted.Search.Term.Counts <- melt(Search.Term.Counts.t[,c("title","string","count")], id=c("title", "string"))
> Search.Term.Counts.Array <- acast(melted.Search.Term.Counts, string ~ title)
>
> # Create the simply flat topic prior
> # alpha here represents the virtual count of times we've seen this topic for this doc (akin to the beta distribution's parameters so that 1 is a flat uniform)

> # loop thru that industry's search terms to appropriately increment the prior for cases of individual terms in a search string of multiple words:

>   Current.Industry.Terms <- subset(Industry.Terms,code == Industry.Code)
>   Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms <- sapply(gregexpr("\\W+", Current.Industry.Terms$string), function(x) sum(x>0) ) + 1
>   Max.Num.Terms <- max(Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms)
>   for (Current.String.Index in 1:nrow(Current.Industry.Terms)) {
>     if (as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]) %in% rownames(Word.Prior)) {
>       Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),Industry.Code] <- Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),Industry.Code] + Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms[Current.String.Index]
>       Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),"000"] <- Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),"000"] + (Max.Num.Terms - Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms[Current.String.Index])
>     }
>   }

> CGS is a really surprisingly good stochastic search algorithm for LDA—it seems to be much easier to optimize the log-likelihood in "z-space" (the word-topic assignments) than in "theta-phi-space" (the topics and topic weights). One reason is sparsity—if you use Dirichlet priors with small hyperparameters and sum out the z variables (which you need to in Stan), then you wind up with a highly nonconvex sparsity-inducing prior. Gradient-based optimization on these kinds of nonconvex problems is very, very hard, and since NUTS relies very heavily on the use of gradient information to tell it where to explore, it's challenging for it to figure out what topics should be active in what documents. (Although in principle it'll figure it out eventually.)
>
> What NUTS is good at is mixing quickly and delivering large numbers of effectively independent samples. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
messages.body_plain:
Mechanically, other than the prior, the uncertainty must come from the data's likelihood. What exactly in the data describes each model parameter is always tough to decipher, particularly with mixtures of distributions... but here goes: the density of each word across documents resembles a mixture of exponential densities and there is a clear covariation in word density across documents (i.e. documents where "gas" appears quite frequently also have "oil" appearing quite frequently); this is what I expect to identify the theta parameters and hence their uncertainty should come from how much the data varies around that signal...

I'm rather certain that each document includes more than 1 topic, although perhaps not every topic appears in each document... So, it still seems to me that LDA is the most appropriate model among those of which I'm aware...

I didn't run out of memory. This takes up about 1GB of memory, of which I still have 10GB free. Interestingly, when I look at the CPU usage of the core handling the process, it reads as only 80% busy...

Theta is the parameter of interest for me; the beta parameters are basically just "nuisance" parameters for my purposes. I want the prior on theta to be completely flat, hence me setting alpha = 1 for all topics. In response to your question, I have revised my model construction in Stan so that the value of alpha fed to Stan no longer varies across documents. I'm not sure why that construction would save computation time since either way alpha = 1 for all topics and documents...

The other change that I made was that initialization that you suggested. Perhaps this produced a serious speed-up? I'm not sure... but, somehow, it ran the first 20 iterations in about 20 minutes. The next 20 iterations took about an hour... and it's still chugging along now...

Yeah, I may have to resort to coding the [fast] CGS myself... or grab someone else's C code and embed it in-line within my r script...

>
> Using LDA for anything other than exploratory data analysis
> seems dangerous.  What do you think the uncertainty is going
> to be characterizing that isn't highly dependent on your prior
> strength in this case?
>
> > It looks like I could "hack" either of those packages to call them repeatedly but the mixing across such iterations may just be so poor that NUTS would be faster.
>
> It's pretty much hopeless trying to mix the multiple modes of LDA.
>
> > More importantly, neither lda or topicmodels is designed to accommodate prior information on how the word distribution differs across topics -- both have just a single parameter for beta (as well as alpha) but my prior knowledge is in how beta differs across topics. Recall that this was my strategy for navigating the multi-modality problems that Bob mentioned (I should be able to keep increasing the strength of my priors until the posterior becomes unimodal).
>
> It still won't be convex, but with enough prior strength
> you can push down the modes you don't want.  You still probably
> won't get proper exploration of the posterior.
>
>
> > To give you more specific detail on my particular problem: my purpose is to estimate the share of each topic discussed in each of 50 documents. I have 50 to 100 pre-determined topics (they are industry names taken from NAICS codes, such as "Oil and Gas Extraction") to which I add an additional topic I call "misc" for none of the above. From these topic descriptions, I have constructed my 1000 to 4000 word vocabulary (e.g. it contains "oil", "gas", "extraction", "oil extraction", and "gas extractrion"). In setting the prior on beta, I can make it so that the word "oil" is more probable than other words when the topic is "oil and gas extraction" (I might have to experiment with how strong it needs to be to ensure that the term "oil" is most associated with "oil and gas extraction", which is what I meant by making the posterior unimodal).
>
> > So, unless there is some way to rehabilitate the lda and/or topicmodels packages, calling stan from r appears to be my only hope short of a radical departure from the comfort of my r platform... well, unless there is some model other than LDA that would be more appropriate here (as an economist, I'm somewhat new to topic models and LDA seemed to be sufficiently appropriate and accepted as a standard approach but I would certainly welcome a better suggestion).
>
> It depends what you're trying to do.  If you are assuming each document
> is made up out of several topics, then LDA's a reasonable model.
>
> But you have to be careful with the prior on the document topic proportions
> (theta in your model and the original LDA papers).  The strength of that prior
> will determine how many topics get non-negligible probability in a document,
> and this in turn plays off against the topic distributions themselves.
>
> > Unfortunately, after letting my machine crunch overnight (approximately 12 hours), stan had made 0 progress on my problem (still on the first iteration).
>
> Do you know if you ran out of memory?  I'd think this would be slow,
> but not 12 hours per iteration slow.
>
> > Here's my stan code (which is slightly modified, from the version in manual that Bob and I discussed, to accommodate a different prior on beta for each topic):

> >   int <lower = 0> K[V,M];           // search term counts in each of the M docs
> >   vector <lower = 0> [T] alpha[M];  // topic prior
>
> Should alpha really vary by document?  Do you have prior information
> on how many topics area in each document?
>
> Given your strong priors, you could try initializing theta and phi
> to the prior means.  alpha / sum(alpha) and beta / sum(beta).
>
> >   vector <lower = 0> [V] beta[T];   // word prior
> > }
> > parameters{
> >   simplex [T] theta[M]; // topic distribution for each of the M docs
> >   simplex [V] phi[T]; // word distribution for each of the T topics
> > }
> > model{
> >   for (m in 1:M)
> >     theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha[m]);  //prior
> >   for (t in 1:T)
> >     phi[t] ~ dirichlet(beta[t]);     //prior
> >   for (v in 1:V) {
> >     for (m in 1:M) {
> >       real gamma [T];
> >       for (t in 1:T)
> >         gamma[t] <- log(theta[m,t]) + log(phi[t,v]); //likelihood
> >       increment_log_prob(K[v,m]*log_sum_exp(gamma));
> >     }
> >   }
> > }
>
> Presumably what you have is very sparse.  So I doubt this will work well.
>
> You might be able to define a collapsed Gibbs sampler for your
> model in JAGS.  Or just write the Gibbs sampler in R directly --- it's
> a pretty easy one.
>
> > Here's my r code that calls stan:

>
> - Bob
>
> >

> > library(reshape2)
> >
> > ##### Import data files
> > Search.Term.Counts <- read.csv("string_title_year_count.csv")
> > Industry.Terms <- read.csv("search_terms_and_industries.csv")
> >
> > # data cleaning: restrict to year 2012 and remove a few negative counts (probably due to a coding mistake upstream)
> > Search.Term.Counts.t <- subset(Search.Term.Counts,year==2012)
> > Search.Term.Counts.t$count <- ifelse(Search.Term.Counts.t$count < 0, 0, Search.Term.Counts.t$count)
> >
> > # extract Num.Words.In.Vocabulary and Num.Docs from Search.Term.Counts
> > Num.Words.In.Vocabulary <- length(levels(Search.Term.Counts.t$string))
> > Num.Docs <- length(levels(as.factor(Search.Term.Counts.t$title)))
> >
> > # extract Num.Topics [= Num.Industries + 1] from Industry.Terms
> > Num.Topics <- length(levels(as.factor(Industry.Terms$code)))+1
> >
> > # extract Search.Term.Counts
> > melted.Search.Term.Counts <- melt(Search.Term.Counts.t[,c("title","string","count")], id=c("title", "string"))
> > Search.Term.Counts.Array <- acast(melted.Search.Term.Counts, string ~ title)
> >
> > # Create the simply flat topic prior
> > # alpha here represents the virtual count of times we've seen this topic for this doc (akin to the beta distribution's parameters so that 1 is a flat uniform)
> > # Steyvers n Griffiths (2007) suggest 50/T, which is actually around 1 here anyway
> > Topic.Prior <- matrix(1,nrow=Num.Topics, ncol=Num.Docs)
> > rownames(Topic.Prior) <- c(levels(as.factor(Industry.Terms$code)),"000")
> > colnames(Topic.Prior) <- levels(as.factor(Search.Term.Counts.t$title))
> >
> > # Create the topic prior which is flat but to which I'll add additional weight allocated for search terms known to be associated with particular industries
> > # beta here represents the virtual count of times we've seen this word used in this topic
> > # Steyvers n Griffiths (2007) suggest 0.01, which is improper, but they acknowledge that it should depend on vocabulary, num docs, etc... so I'll stick with 1 that corresponds to a flat uniform
> > Word.Prior <- matrix(1,nrow=Num.Words.In.Vocabulary, ncol=Num.Topics)
> > rownames(Word.Prior) <- levels(Search.Term.Counts.t$string)
> > colnames(Word.Prior) <- c(levels(as.factor(Industry.Terms$code)),"000")
> >
> > # add information to the word prior
> > # loop thru each industry (not including the misc topic category)
> > # find the maximum number of words in that industry's search terms
> > # loop thru that industry's search terms to appropriately increment the prior for cases of individual terms in a search string of multiple words:
> > # the individual word should be more associated with misc and the whole search string of multiple words should be more associated with the industry
> > for (Current.Industry.Index in 1:(ncol(Word.Prior)-1)) {
> >   Industry.Code <- colnames(Word.Prior)[Current.Industry.Index]
> >   Current.Industry.Terms <- subset(Industry.Terms,code == Industry.Code)
> >   Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms <- sapply(gregexpr("\\W+", Current.Industry.Terms$string), function(x) sum(x>0) ) + 1
> >   Max.Num.Terms <- max(Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms)
> >   for (Current.String.Index in 1:nrow(Current.Industry.Terms)) {
> >     if (as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]) %in% rownames(Word.Prior)) {
> >       Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),Industry.Code] <- Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),Industry.Code] + Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms[Current.String.Index]
> >       Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),"000"] <- Word.Prior[as.character(Current.Industry.Terms$string[Current.String.Index]),"000"] + (Max.Num.Terms - Current.Industry.Terms$Num.Terms[Current.String.Index])
> >     }
> >   }
> > }
> >
> >
> > ##########################################################################################
> > # Analyze with Stan
> > ##########################################################################################
> >
> > # reshaping the data as required by Stan -- packed into a list: counts as a VxM array, topic prior as a TxM array, and word prior as a VxM array
> > StanInputData <- list(T = Num.Topics, V = Num.Words.In.Vocabulary, M = Num.Docs, K = Search.Term.Counts.Array, alpha = t(Topic.Prior), beta = t(Word.Prior))
> >
> > # run stan on the file, compile to C [stanc()], and iteratively draw samples from the posterior [sampling()]
> > stan.fit <- stan(file="LDA.stan", data=StanInputData, seed = 12345, iter=1000, chains=4)
> >
> >
> >

> > On Thu, Aug 28, 2014 at 10:22 PM, Matt Hoffman <mdho...@cs.princeton.edu> wrote:
> > Stan can be used to fit LDA. But you may be disappointed if you compare its ability to find good parameters quickly with a standard collapsed Gibbs sampler.
> >

> > CGS is a really surprisingly good stochastic search algorithm for LDA--it seems to be much easier to optimize the log-likelihood in "z-space" (the word-topic assignments) than in "theta-phi-space" (the topics and topic weights). One reason is sparsity--if you use Dirichlet priors with small hyperparameters and sum out the z variables (which you need to in Stan), then you wind up with a highly nonconvex sparsity-inducing prior. Gradient-based optimization on these kinds of nonconvex problems is very, very hard, and since NUTS relies very heavily on the use of gradient information to tell it where to explore, it's challenging for it to figure out what topics should be active in what documents. (Although in principle it'll figure it out eventually.)
> >
> > What NUTS is good at is mixing quickly and delivering large numbers of effectively independent samples. Nobody really knows what the mixing speed of CGS is like, and most people don't care--for most topic modeling applications people aren't really interested in quantifying the uncertainty in their parameter estimates.

> > >

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
messages.body_plain:
> I'm a researcher, so uncertainty matters to me because producing just a point estimate wouldn't be acceptable for publication (for good reason, IMHO).

Given that mixing across the combinatorially explosive number of modes for a model like LDA is impossible, any estimate of posterior uncertainty you wind up with is likely to be at best a very loose lower bound. As Bob said, the source of this multimodality is not just label-switching, but also the sparsity induced by the Dirichlet distribution. Reporting posterior-based confidence intervals may therefore be more misleading than not including any confidence intervals at all.

Perhaps you can describe the specific question you're trying to answer and get uncertainty estimates about?

> Theta is the parameter of interest for me; the beta parameters are basically just "nuisance" parameters for my purposes. I want the prior on theta to be completely flat, hence me setting alpha = 1 for all topics.

FYI, this isn't an "uninformative" prior. Like all priors on the simplex, it corresponds to a very specific set of assumptions about how many topics you expect to see per document.

A less rigid approach would be to learn the prior on theta, as suggested by Wallach et al. in "Rethinking LDA: Why Priors Matter":
https://people.cs.umass.edu/~wallach/publications/wallach09rethinking.pdf

Matt

You're right, I'd want to be clear about that. I thought that my prior scheme would also rule out the sparsity-induced multi-modality. If every Dirichlet parameter is greater than or equal to 1 then it should be unimodal in the simplex. Again, I could be missing something...

Matt, I sent you a private email about my particular application, which is unlikely to be of interest to the broader user group...

Yeah, if the Dirichlet parameters are all equal to 1, then the prior is uniform in the simplex. Such an assumption increases the appeal of Bayesian work to an audience dominated by frequentists because it makes the posterior proportional to the data's likelihood (with which they are comfortable). However, you're right that any prior corresponds to a very specification set of assumptions about how many topics we'd expect to see (a priori) in a document. Hence, flat isn't exactly uninformative, which can be seen via a reparameterization of the model.

I found the approach proposed by Wallach et al. (2009), ie optimization with respect to the prior parameters, to be rather appealing; however, I didn't immediately understand the intuition behind their results. I would have thought that the (abstract) symmetry in the problem would result in the symmetric-asymmetric prior being just as good as the asymmetric-symmetric prior. That said, if I tried to wholely adopt their recommended approach, then I would lose the ability to incorporate my prior information (which, intuitively, is the whole purpose of a prior) and I may not be able to cleanly assign the pre-determined topic names to the latent topics generated... By the way, I noticed that this Wallach et al. (2009) approach had been implemented in the c code that Janne Sinkkonen linked to (hca: http://mloss.org/software/view/527/)... that site also references a new paper (Li et al. 2014) which seems very promising for speeding up LDA (see: http://www.sravi.org/pubs/fastlda-kdd2014.pdf)...

messages.body_plain:
On Sep 1, 2014, at 12:11 PM, Bentley Coffey <bentley...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Mechanically, other than the prior, the uncertainty must come from the data's likelihood. What exactly in the data describes each model parameter is always tough to decipher, particularly with mixtures of distributions... but here goes: the density of each word across documents resembles a mixture of exponential densities and there is a clear covariation in word density across documents (i.e. documents where "gas" appears quite frequently also have "oil" appearing quite frequently); this is what I expect to identify the theta parameters and hence their uncertainty should come from how much the data varies around that signal...

I'd suggest doing a sensitivity analysis with different priors.
They make a huge difference in terms of the implicit correlation
among words being modeled.  High count priors in alpha spread
out each document, which in effect shrinks all the topic models
and lessens the correlation effect in the posterior.

LDA's pretty good at modeling the burstiness of words across
documents, but you'll need to tune the priors heavily if you
expect it to be well calibrated to new data in the language
modeling sense of making good predictions (high probability) for
new documents.

> I'm rather certain that each document includes more than 1 topic, although perhaps not every topic appears in each document... So, it still seems to me that LDA is the most appropriate model among those of which I'm aware...
>
> I didn't run out of memory. This takes up about 1GB of memory, of which I still have 10GB free. Interestingly, when I look at the CPU usage of the core handling the process, it reads as only 80% busy...
>
> Theta is the parameter of interest for me; the beta parameters are basically just "nuisance" parameters for my purposes. I want the prior on theta to be completely flat, hence me setting alpha = 1 for all topics.

I often see people use alpha << 1 to avoid the following issue.

Suppose you have 100 words in a document and 100 topics.
And you see 10 words in one topic, 30 in a second, and
60 in a third.  Then you get 11/200, 31/200, and 61/200
posterior mean probabilities and about half the posterior
mass assigned to the 97 "out-of-topic" topics.

> In response to your question, I have revised my model construction in Stan so that the value of alpha fed to Stan no longer varies across documents. I'm not sure why that construction would save computation time since either way alpha = 1 for all topics and documents...

It won't save time.  I just wondered why it was varying.

> The other change that I made was that initialization that you suggested. Perhaps this produced a serious speed-up?

It can if a random init is way out in the tails.

> I'm not sure... but, somehow, it ran the first 20 iterations in about 20 minutes. The next 20 iterations took about an hour... and it's still chugging along now...

It goes over a hump in the early iterations when it gets serious about
setting both the mass matrix and the step size.  Then it should speed up.

> Yeah, I may have to resort to coding the [fast] CGS myself... or grab someone else's C code and embed it in-line within my r script...

You probably don't even need to do it in C.  But
you'd need to customize it to deal with varying priors.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Sep 1, 2014, at 12:02 PM, Martin Šmíra <smira....@gmail.com> wrote:

> I actually want to use Matt trick in a hierarchical reinforcement-learning I brought up 2 weeks ago. Maybe you still remember, it's here: https://groups.google.com/forum/?hl=cs#!topic/stan-users/TjY3wQqUS2g
>
> I want to use Matt trick in the mixture part there. Would it be any use?

I'm not sure.  One thing to think about is whether you
need separate normal(0,1) underlying raw parameters for
each of the mixture components.  The suggestion I made a couple
days ago re-used the same one, but I'm not sure that's right
as it'll keep the multiple modes in lock step in the posterior.

The main reason to try it would be poor mixing of hierarchical
prior parameters.

> I tried to implement softmax as you suggested, but the performance didn't really improve.
>
> Since we're again talking about this model, you recommended us to use inv_logit instead of Phi, but it turned out that after this change model gives quite different posteriors for parameters of interest. Is Phi_approx also good choice here?

The parameters will be scaled differently with inv_logit and
Phi, but the effect should be roughly the same in terms of
regression predictions.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] how to constrain the sum of variables to stay positive
messages.body_plain:
On Aug 30, 2014, at 4:55 PM, Jonathan Gilligan <jonathan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I have a related problem:
>
> I have a parameter, gamma, that must be greater than zero. I can fit the model to the data very nicely with something like:
>
> theta <- 0.0;
>
> for (i in 1:N) {
>   theta <- theta + ( ( gain[i] ^alpha - 1.0) / alpha - (lambda * loss[i]^beta - 1.0 ) / beta ) * p^gamma / (p^gamma + (1.0-p)^gamma)^( 1.0 / gamma);
> }
>
> data ~ bernoulli_logit( scale_factor * theta )
>
> where gain, loss, and p are data and alpha, beta, gamma, and scale_factor are parameters. This converges nicely and I a sensible posterior for gamma. Then I try to explain gamma in terms of demographic covariates:
>
> gamma <- b_sex * sex + b_age * age + b_household_size * household_size
>
> where b_xxx are parameters and sex, age, etc. are data. I expect that some of the b_ parameters will be positive and some will be negative, so I don't want to constrain them to all be positive; but I would need to constrain the dot product of b with the demographic variables to be positive.

> I didn't see a way to constrain the sum of the b_ coefficients times the data to be positive and everything I did led to horrible performance and failure to converge.

So you want to select coefficients that guarantee gamma is positive?
If household_size > 0 in all cases, you can do it with a minimum
on b_household_size.  You can write a function to compute the minimum
and then use it in the constraint.

> I can get this to converge if I put very restrictive priors on the individual coefficients, but if I do that, then my results would just be fine-tuning my priors and I don't have enough actual prior knowledge of these parameters to justify that.
>
> The folk theorem has led me to try a using different model for probability weighting, whose parameters don't need to be constrained this way, but that introduces its own complications because the original model is the Kahneman-Tversky model of probability weighting for cumulative prospect theory, so using a different model for probability weighting would mean my analysis would break with most of the literature from the last two decades simply for computational reasons, and that makes me uncomfortable.

How do people usually deal with this kind of constraint?

I'm used to seeing link functions in GLMs that enforce the
right signs on everythnig (e.g., inv_logit for logistic regression
and exp for poisson).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: waic
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: waic
messages.body_plain:
You can use the same approach for WAIC as for cross-validation. See section 2.3 in Aki Vehtari and Jouko Lampinen (2002). Bayesian model assessment and comparison using cross-validation predictive densities. Neural Computation, 14(10):2439-2468. http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/publications/VehtariLampinen_NC2002_preprint.pdf  This works very well when p_eff << n/2.  If p_eff is relatively high compared to n, the approach provides a useful indicator, but it's not so well calibrated (we are investigating this).

I have also used thumb rules similar to what, e.g,  Burnham and Anderson mention. Often they work, but sometimes there is much more variation in WAIC (or CV) estimates and these thumb rules can then be misleading. Usually this happens if there are a small number of observations with a very low predictive density, ie. they are far in the tails of the predictive distribution and even small changes in the model can change the predictive density a lot for these.

Aki

On Aug 30, 2014, at 3:01 PM, Katherine Grace Jonas <katherine....@gmail.com> wrote:

> The constraint is essentially an ordering constraint.  The model is an graded response IRT model, in which category thresholds are decomposed into a item-specific and person-specific component.  The item thresholds can be declared as an ordered vector.  The person components are not necessarily ordered, but the sum of the person and item components is an ordered vector.  So each person component depends on the distance between item thresholds and the adjacent person component.  For example, if the minimum distance between two item thresholds is z, and the person components of those two thresholds are x and y, respectively, then x < z + y.
>
> I've tried declaring a (person x item x category) array of ordered vectors, but it becomes prohibitively large.  Declaring the array as a local variable would work, but it looks like local variables need to be basic variable types.

In transformed data and transformed parameters, the constraints are just consistency tests.
For parameters, they implicitly perform a transform to unconstrained representations
and include the log Jacobian in the log probability function.

> It's tricky, but I think the constraint is coming from a reasonable assumption: that individuals may differ in the extent to which they are willing to endorse "good" versus "very good," (or some similar categories), but that those tendencies do not change the rank ordering of categories.

Does each person use the same regression coefficients to produce
a latent "quality" score and then just have different cutpoints?

Otherwise, I don't see how you could maintain the same ordering across
items.

I don't even see how that'd make sense in a context like grading stage of
tumor --- two different doctors might order two tumor images differently
in terms of cancer stage.

And if you look at something like the Netflix challenge data
with customer ratings, there was wildly different orderings among
customers of movies.

Andrew Gelman and Jennifer Hill discuss models with cutpoints varying
by individual in their regression book.  And I just happen to know Andrew's
been thinking more about priors --- we'll probably be discussing next week
in the Stan meeting and then coming out with some recommendations in
the next manual for hierarchical priors on the cutpoints.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Firstly, 2047 is indicative of hitting the max_depth threshold in NUTS which will cause
large autocorrelations.  You should increase max_depth, but as Bob notes you’re only
hitting the threshold because the step size is so small.  This can very likely be due to
large curvature changes near the discontinuity.

The thing you have to realize with HMC is that the algorithm doesn’t suffer only when
the trajectory hits the discontinuity.  Every time the trajectory _passes_ the discontinuity
it should jump a bit, but we can’t simulate that and the resulting trajectories start to
drift from the true posterior.  Short answer — discontinuities are bad and, in particular,
all of our adaptation is not guaranteed to work any more.  Make your model smooth
by ensuring that the first derivatives match at the transition between the two regions.

Also, any continuous model with any n_divergent=1 iterations are bad.  You should
revisit those and decrease the step size until the divergent iterations go away.

messages.body_plain:
The log probability function and its gradient should
be continuous.

Michael's talking about the problems you get when the gradients
are not continous.  For instance,

  fabs(x) = |x|

is continuous, but its derivative

  d/dx fabs(x) = 1 if x > 0
                -1 if x < 0
                undefined if x = 0

is undefined at 0 and there's no way to fill in a value to
make it continuous.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] how to constrain the sum of variables to stay positive
messages.body_plain:
Is there a reason you can't make a hierarchical model where
there's a population distribution of cutpoints then an
individual varies from that?  Then each cutpoint gets a prior
in the ordered vector.  As in:

parameters {
  ordered[K] mu;
  ordered[K] c[J];
  real<lower=0> sigma[K];
  ...
}
model {
  mu ~ some prior;

  for (j in 1:J)

    c[j,k] ~ normal(mu[k], sigma[k]);
  ...
}

This essentially makes c[j,k] the sum of mu[k] and an epsilon[j,k].  In
regression terms:

   c[j,k] = mu[k] + epsilon[j,k];
   epsilon[j,k] ~ normal(0,sigma[k]);

I think this does the same thing, puts it in the context of a hierarchical
model, and maintains all the appropriate ordering constraints.

I'd be inclined to start with a single sigma, then have varying sigma,
then try to move to a hierarchical model for the sigma, as well.

I'm a little unclear on what a good prior for mu is.  It should
be strongly identified for location and scale, though, whatever it is.

- Bob

messages.subject: ideas for future stan development
messages.subject_clean: ideas for future stan development
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

As many of us I have started my travel to stan starting with WinBUGS.  I found stan modeling environment quite flexible.  I wonder if it makes sense to implement in stan sampling algorithms such as Gibbs sampling, Generalized Direct Sampling.  In additional to sampling based algorithms implementation of deterministic algorithms such as Expectation Propagation might be useful.  Specifically, at Purdue University, we have developed an algorithm based on KL optimization. Many of those algorithms require likelihood function which may become a nasty looking function if you try to code in R.  A common modeling language framework as well as diversity of algorithms would be great.

Another idea is to remove PK modeling gap.  While WinBUGS has PKBugs for PK modeling, stan currently doesn't have this capability. I know that there are some thoughts but it would be nice to have this capability sooner.

Thanks,
Linas

probably be the first one done.  It's being taken on by Alp Kucukelbir

the just-finished higher-order autodiff, which will be out in Stan 2.5.

prototyped and has just been awaiting higher-order autodiff being done;

Stan 2.5!  The final draft version is currently unit testing
in my other window.  It was a pretty substantial effort because
we need derivatives of the solutions in order to do HMC and
gradient-based optimization.

We also have plans to write wrappers for PK/PD applications in
particular.  Here's a link to a PK/PD project we did with Novartis on
a prototype implementation directly in C++ coupled with some nifty
meta-analysis:

http://www.page-meeting.org/?abstract=3200

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: What is the largest model you've used with Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Hello group,

Obviously the mere dimensionality of a problem doesn't fully determine the speed of convergence of a MCMC. The correlation between the variables, the complexity of the model, etc all play important roles.

That said, I'm trying to get a sense of the order of magnitude of the size of problems that have a chance to be tackled.

Is it sensible to use Stan on a model with hundreds of parameters? Tens of thousands? Millions?

Some of the default behaviors of cmdstan (such as printing each parameter for each sample) suggest that the typical models have at most dozens of parameters. Is that so?

Thanks,
Arthur

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] What is the largest model you've used with Stan?
messages.body_plain:
The examples are misleading because most of them are from
textbooks that have kept things simple and small.

We've fit simple models like IRT with millions of parameters,
but it takes a few hours.  We regularly fit all kinds of
models with thousands of parameters.

CmdStan saves each sample (but can be set to thin).  We're
thinking about adding something to CmdStan like RStan has
that will let you suppress output for some variables.

If the saved output is too big, it can choke our posterior
analysis tools.  But that's a different problem than the
sampler not working.  You can still easily do things like
compute posterior means and sd using online algorithms like
Welford's and you can do pretty well at getting wide
intervals (50% intervals require saving half the samples online,
whereas 5% intervals only require saving 5% in memory).

If you want to do logistic regression with L1 regularization
and millions of parameters and billions of sparse training instances,
you'll need to use something more specialized like Vowpal Wabbit.
Of course, there's a problem with summarizing output given their
hashing, but again, that's a different problem than being able to
fit the model.

- Bob

Bob,

Thanks for taking the time to read and advise me on this model.

I ran something similar to what you suggested, but incorporating multiple items (where i indexes items, n indexes respondents, and k indexes categories):

parameters {
ordered[K-1] c_i[I];
ordered[K-1] c_ni[N,I];
...other parameters...
}
model {
...prior on item cutpoints...

for (n in 1:N) {
  for (i in 1:I) {
    for (k in 1:(K-1)) {
    c_ni[n,i,k] ~ normal(c_i[i,k],c_n_sigma[k]);
    }
  }
}
c_n_sigma ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

As soon as I started running this, though, I realized the model would draw a new person parameter for each category for each item (N x I x K parameters).  How can I write this to sample N x K parameters, while maintaining the ordering constraint on the N x I x K array?  I tried:

for (n in 1:N) {
  for (k in 1:(K-1)) {
  segment(c_ni[n],1,I-1)[k] ~ normal(0,c_n_sigma[k]) + col(c_i,k);
  }
}

But arithmetic on the right side of the sampling statement throws an error.

On Wednesday, September 3, 2014 11:53:07 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Is there a reason you can't make a hierarchical model where
> there's a population distribution of cutpoints then an
> individual varies from that?  Then each cutpoint gets a prior
> in the ordered vector.  As in:
>
> parameters {
>   ordered[K] mu;
>   ordered[K] c[J];
>   real<lower=0> sigma[K];
>   ...
> }
> model {
>   mu ~ some prior;
>   for (j in 1:J)
>     c[j,k] ~ normal(mu[k], sigma[k]);
>   ...
> }
>
> This essentially makes c[j,k] the sum of mu[k] and an epsilon[j,k].  In
> regression terms:
>
>    c[j,k] = mu[k] + epsilon[j,k];
>    epsilon[j,k] ~ normal(0,sigma[k]);
>
> I think this does the same thing, puts it in the context of a hierarchical
> model, and maintains all the appropriate ordering constraints.
>
> I'd be inclined to start with a single sigma, then have varying sigma,
> then try to move to a hierarchical model for the sigma, as well.
>
> I'm a little unclear on what a good prior for mu is.  It should
> be strongly identified for location and scale, though, whatever it is.
>

So the cutpoints in the ordered logistic distribution are the sum of an ordered vector and a vector of normally distributed person components.

> > >
> > > > The constraint is essentially an ordering constraint.  The model is an graded response IRT model, in which category thresholds are decomposed into a item-specific and person-specific component.  The item thresholds can be declared as an ordered vector.  The person components are not necessarily ordered, but the sum of the person and item components is an ordered vector.  So each person component depends on the distance between item thresholds and the adjacent person component.  For example, if the minimum distance between two item thresholds is z, and the person components of those two thresholds are x and y, respectively, then x < z + y.
> > > >

> > > For parameters, they implicitly perform a transform to unconstrained representations
> > > and include the log Jacobian in the log probability function.

> > >
> > > And if you look at something like the Netflix challenge data
> > > with customer ratings, there was wildly different orderings among
> > > customers of movies.
> > >

I meant that the categories themselves maintain an order (i.e. all doctor's agree that the stage II label should indicate a cancer is more progressed than a stage I cancer, and all Netflix raters agree that a three star rating should be used to indicate that they like a movie better than a two star rating). messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: unable to install stan 2.4
messages.body_plain:
I had previously had issues for RStan 2.1 due to being behind a corporate firewall. I had resolved them (with some help from the mailing list) by a solution similar to what has been described here. However, as a result of getting a new computer, I had to do a fresh install and what I did before doesn't seem to be working now. After setwding to the correct folder, I ran the

install.packages("rstan_2.4.0.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")

and get a message about RCpp, inline, RCppEigen, and BH not being available. This is in spite of them all loading successfully on their own. However, I realized that I was using the lib.loc feature when loading them. I had used the packages from a location different from what RStan is used to. So then I installed them all to the default locations and re-ran the install rstan command, and now it works.

These dependencies are no longer noted in the Getting Started RStan page (and I only was aware of RCpp and inline from before, I think RCppEigen and BH are new, I had downloaded and re-tried without getting them to work).

messages.subject: Re: What is the largest model you've used with Stan?
messages.subject_clean: What is the largest model you've used with Stan?
messages.body_plain:
I think the largest number of parameters I've used in a Stan model is about 30k. It worked just fine.

In fact, sometimes I add parameters by taking out e.g. marginalization and it actually fits better. Earlier this year, I worked a hidden Markov model with gamma latency emissions with lots of censoring, and just estimating the censored values as missing with known constraint lead to slightly better mixing than using the gamma ccdf, even though it added lots of parameters to the posterior.

On Thursday, September 4, 2014 4:18:32 PM UTC-7, Arthur B. wrote:
> Hello group,
>
> Obviously the mere dimensionality of a problem doesn't fully determine the speed of convergence of a MCMC. The correlation between the variables, the complexity of the model, etc all play important roles.
>
> That said, I'm trying to get a sense of the order of magnitude of the size of problems that have a chance to be tackled.
>
> Is it sensible to use Stan on a model with hundreds of parameters? Tens of thousands? Millions?
>
> Some of the default behaviors of cmdstan (such as printing each parameter for each sample) suggest that the typical models have at most dozens of parameters. Is that so?
>
> Thanks,
> Arthur
>

messages.body_plain:
The default for HMC is to estimate a diagonal mass
matrix during warmup.  You can override that and have
it estimate a full mass matrix or just take a unit
mass matrix.  The default for optimization is to use
L-BFGS which approximates a Hessian using a finite history
of gradients, but never needs to store the whole matrix or
do an inversion.

We haven't found many problems where a dense mass matrix
is helpful.

Feel free to ask on the list about how things work now --- some
of the historical notes are now just that.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I items, N respondents, K categories (so K - 1 cutpoints).

parameters {
  ordered[K-1] mu_c;
  ordered[K-1] c[N];
}
model {
  c_mu ~ normal(0,5);
  sigma_c ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

  for (n in 1:N)

    c[n] ~ normal(mu_c, sigma_c);
}

mu_c:  population cutpoints

c[n] : cut points for respondent n

Then presumably the score for the item would be based
on a regression and the observed response would use
the cutpoints c[n].  The regression coefficients can also
be modeled hierarchically, as in:

data {
  row_vector[M] x[I];  // predictors for item i
  int<lower=1,upper=K> y[N,I];  // respondent n category for item i

parameters {
  ...
  vector[M] mu_beta;  // prior mean coeffs
  vector[M] beta[N];  // coeffs for respondent n

model {
  ...
  mu_beta ~ normal(0,5);
  sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  beta ~ normal(mu_beta, sigma_beta);

  for (i in 1:I)

    for (n in 1:N)
      y[i,n] ~ ordered_logistic(x[i] * beta[n], c[n]);

I'm not sure that's well enough identified, though.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
It's possible using optimization.  It's easier in R/Python than
from the command line.

Having said that, Stan usually converges quickly from diffuse
starting points.  Running multiple such chains and getting to
the same end point is a further check that you're really
at convergence.

Also, many models of interest, such as hierarchical models,
do not have posterior modes (density approaches infinity as
hierarchical variance approaches zero and the low-level parameters
approach the hierarchical mean).  In those cases, it's possible
to only iterate the L-BFGS solver for optimization a few iterations,
but you're in uncharted waters.  Do report back if you go there
and survive and have advice for the rest of us.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] how to constrain the sum of variables to stay positive
messages.body_plain:
If two vectors are both ordered and you add them, the result's
still ordered.

- Bob

messages.subject: Problem with multimodality (Dirichlet parameters in one chain stuck near 0)
messages.subject_clean: Problem with multimodality (Dirichlet parameters in one chain stuck near 0)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am estimating a version of a dynamic ecological inference model. The model allows future information on interior cell proportions to inform estimates for other periods when only the marginal proportions are observed. It does so with a Dirichlet transition model for the cell proportions, as in:
props[t] ~ dirichlet(props[t - 1] * priorN);
I use a uniform prior for the proportions in t=1.

Stan usually handles the model fine, but when I estimate it with 10 chains, 9 of the chains will converge on a single mode but one chain often gets stuck in a different part of the parameter space. The posterior means looks something like this:
          parameters
chains     props[1,1] props[1,2] props[1,3] props[1,4] props[1,5] props[1,6] props[1,7] props[1,8]
  chain:1   0.4092150  0.0170668  0.3179837  0.0093268  0.1372389  0.0564969  0.0469633  0.0057086
  chain:2   0.4097358  0.0165229  0.3174619  0.0098698  0.1373309  0.0564284  0.0468729  0.0057774
  chain:3   0.4093795  0.0169492  0.3178193  0.0094436  0.1372392  0.0564494  0.0469648  0.0057550
  chain:4   0.4093129  0.0170535  0.3178883  0.0093397  0.1372275  0.0564268  0.0469739  0.0057774
  chain:5   0.4092606  0.0170692  0.3179373  0.0093230  0.1372526  0.0564344  0.0469514  0.0057716
  chain:6   0.4091285  0.0171836  0.3180702  0.0092095  0.1372895  0.0564151  0.0469134  0.0057903
  chain:7   0.5577684  0.0000012  0.1694708  0.0263796  0.0000001  0.0622129  0.1841663  0.0000007
  chain:8   0.4094046  0.0169750  0.3177931  0.0094183  0.1372448  0.0563948  0.0469588  0.0058106
  chain:9   0.4092455  0.0170548  0.3179528  0.0093383  0.1372717  0.0564431  0.0469317  0.0057621
  chain:10  0.4091930  0.0170815  0.3180064  0.0093115  0.1372493  0.0564916  0.0469537  0.0057131
As you can see, in chain 7 proportions 2, 5, and 8 are stuck very close to 0. These aberrant values are not only far from the consensus among the other chains, but also implausible in light of the interior cell information from other periods.

Obviously, I could deal with this by simply throwing out the aberrant chains, but I am curious (1) what is causing the problems and (2) whether there is an easy solution. One idea I had is to use a slightly informative prior, but I am reluctant to add too much prior information as it would be difficult to do in a principled way.

Thanks for your help!
Devin

messages.body_plain:
Right.  The trick is the item cutpoints are ordered, and (item cutpoints + person components) are ordered, but the person cutpoints themselves are not necessarily ordered (i.e. c[n,1] could be positive while c[n,3] is negative, resulting in a greater than average tendency to rate something as either 1 or 4, as opposed to 2 or 3).  So it has to be some constraint that results in ordered + vector = ordered.

messages.body_plain:
This is not multimodality but rather a failure of convergence.  In particular, you should be seeing n_divergent=1
for many, if not most, iterations.  The problem is the extreme curvature near zero which causes the gradients,
and hence the HMC transitions, to fail.

An immediate option is to decrease the step size (or increase the target average acceptance probability in the
adaptation).  Alternatively you can try to find a parameterization that reduces the change in curvature.  Lastly
you can reduce the curvature by smoothing out your model, as you have done.

for (t in 1:T) {

  if (t > 1) {
    logit_props[t] ~ normal(logit_props[t - 1], innovation_sd);

Hi Richard,

Thanks for clarifying. Do you have any idea why adding parameters for censored values yielded better mixing, compared to integrating out the censored values? Could it be a results of potential differences in numerical stability of the PDF and CDF functions in Stan? E.g., the CDF function normal_cdf_log will default to -Inf for (y-mu)/sigma < 8.25, which may happen for censored values if the model's expected value for said value is well above the censoring threshold (assuming left-censoring in this case) and sigma is not too large. The manual does not state anything about the numerical stability of normal_log, but if it's more stable than the CDF (i.e. it defaults to -Inf for z << 8.25), it might explain things.

Or maybe there's an entirely different explanation for the better mixing you report?

I've been having mixing issues with a model for data that are partly left-censored. In this model I ise the lognormal_cdf_log function to integrate out censored values.. It'd be great if using the PDF (effectively truncated by the constraints on the parameter) could help there, though it will be pain to code as the observations in the data have been censored at different values (hopefully we'll be able to use vectors of values for parameters constraints in the near future).

Thanks,

Luc

messages.body_plain:
> To follow up again: I tried setting adapt_delta to .9, .95, and .99, and it didn't seem to affect the output.

Did the final step size drop?  The dependence of the final step size on the target average acceptance probability is highly nonlinear so you may have to turn adaptation off and set the step size yourself.

> One or two chains would always get stuck somewhere far from the others. Also, the problem doesn't seem to have much to do with n_divergent.

Yes, it does. Basically n_divergent != 0 indicates that there is a pathological region of phase space and with some probability any chain will eventually get stuck (or run long enough and the probability that it will get stuck at least once goes to unity).  It’s not the proportion of 1s, it’s whether you see any at all (technically, the proportion is more related to how big the pathological region is).

If you ran and saw a nontrivial number of divergent iterations but none of the chains got stuck that doesn’t mean the results are valid — you just lucked out and didn’t get stuck.  The expectations are still biased.

> In every chain, n_divergent=1 in 2–5% of iterations, and the proportion of 1s appeared to be unrelated to getting stuck. Specifying a more informative prior is more effective at avoiding the problem but isn't fool-proof. Also, I should clarify that I was already declaring props as a simplex, and that I am using rstan Version 2.4.0.

More informative priors soften the curvature changes around the boundary and you should see the proportion of n_divergent iterations drop correspondingly.  Typically these kinds of problems arise in hierarchical models and we get around them with non-centered parameterizations, but without seeing your model it’s not clear if there would be an equivalent reparameterization.

> > One or two chains would always get stuck somewhere far from the others. Also, the problem doesn't seem to have much to do with n_divergent.
>
> Yes, it does. Basically n_divergent != 0 indicates that there is a pathological region of phase space and with some probability any chain will eventually get stuck (or run long enough and the probability that it will get stuck at least once goes to unity).  It’s not the proportion of 1s, it’s whether you see any at all (technically, the proportion is more related to how big the pathological region is).
>
> If you ran and saw a nontrivial number of divergent iterations but none of the chains got stuck that doesn’t mean the results are valid — you just lucked out and didn’t get stuck.  The expectations are still biased.
>
> > In every chain, n_divergent=1 in 2–5% of iterations, and the proportion of 1s appeared to be unrelated to getting stuck. Specifying a more informative prior is more effective at avoiding the problem but isn't fool-proof. Also, I should clarify that I was already declaring props as a simplex, and that I am using rstan Version 2.4.0.
>
> More informative priors soften the curvature changes around the boundary and you should see the proportion of n_divergent iterations drop correspondingly.  Typically these kinds of problems arise in hierarchical models and we get around them with non-centered parameterizations, but without seeing your model it’s not clear if there would be an equivalent reparameterization.

messages.body_plain:
> Thanks again for the clarification, Michael. As you can tell, I have many things to learn about how Stan actually works on the inside.

We’re learning, too.  A lot of the practical advice is coming from the latest things we’ve learned about HMC heoretically and much of it is relatively novel for typical MCMC algorithms.

> Your response makes me think that if I can't completely eliminate the n_divergent = 1 problem, maybe the best solution is simply to run multiple chains and throw out the ones that get stuck.

This is what you absolutely don’t want to do.

Let’s assume that the pathological region is around a boundary at zero.  What the divergences are telling you is that there is a small region near zero with significant probability mass that will effect all of your Monte Carlo estimates, but the step size of the sampler is too large for HMC to be able to explore that region.  Most of the time the region just gets ignored, and occasionally the sampler will be in just the right position to jump into the region but then it cannot escape.  In either case the resulting expectations will be biased so none of the chains will be valid.

Unless all of your chains report n_divergent=0 we cannot guarantee the accuracy of your Monte Carlo estimates.

Incidentally, this kind of pathology occurs in Random Walk Metropolis and the Gibbs sampler, too, only there’s rarely an indication that something is going wrong (no n_divergent equivalent).  At least HMC is informing us that something is afoul!

> By the way, I don't know how to check the final step size, so I don't know whether increasing adapt_delta to 0.99 succeeded in decreasing it.

The step size should be output in the summary call.  I’m not an RStan user myself so I won’t be of much help here.

Yeah, the problem in these cases can be that warmup never explored the pathological region enough to adapt the step size correctly.  Try turning adaptation off and setting the step size directly (starting with whatever the nominal step size is now) and decreasing by factors of 2 until the divergences go away.  The only problem here is that you loose the adaption of the metric — in your current runs are you seeing metric components far away from 1?

messages.subject: A few ideas for future versions...
messages.subject_clean: A few ideas for future versions...
messages.body_plain:
I thought I'd just share a few ideas for Stan. I'm still fairly new to the software, so I may misunderstand some of the features. Some of those ideas are likely to have been floated before, and I appreciate that the development team doesn't have unlimited resources.

That said, perhaps this can be the start of a useful conversation.

General
------------

- Support for sparse covariance matrices / band diagonal Cholesky matrices would be swell for implementing some Gaussian processes, such as AR(p). Alternatively, supporting vector and array slicing could confer the same benefit.

- Support for Daubechies wavelets and FFT is also useful to model large arrays with few coefficients.

- Some functions such as sqrt aren't yet vectorized.

Sampling
---------------

- l-bfgs-hmc looks quite promising and seems much cheaper than Riemannian HMC.

- parallel tempering is big in molecular dynamics where finding where the mass of the distribution lies is half the battle. Any thoughts on it?

Modeling language
-------------------------------

- Why not use name mangling to limit accidental collisions with C++ keywords?

- Parameters and generated quantities could be annotated to specify the sampler's behavior
(@all: keep track of variable / @m[k]: keep track of the first k moments only / @category: keep track of the marginal categorical distribution of the parameter / @ignore: ignore)

- If I'm not mistaken, upper and lower bounds only seem to apply during initialization and aren't enforced later on, unless T[] is used. The semantic is a little bit confusing as the bound is applied to the parameter's type, suggesting it's an intrinsic property. If it is only used for initialization, it should appear on the right hand side.

Python specific
-------------------------

- It would be very useful to be able to build a python representation of the model, before compilation, for debugging purposes. Beats "print".

- Is there a way to pass a logger to the sampling method instead of having it write to stdout by default?

Best,
Arthur

For every observation i, you need to do log_sum_exp(ps[1] + multi_normal_log (y[i], a_mu, a_Sigma), ps[2] + multi_normal_log (y[i], b_mu, b_Sigma)). That is the entire likelihood for the data y.

You might want to tighten those priors for a_mu and b_mu, unless you believe this to appropriately reflect the scale of your expectation. Also, your variance-covariance matrices still need to be properly constrained.

messages.body_plain:
The following line your code (in the loop) does not make sense as it will always evaluate to zero: increment_log_prob (log_sum_exp (log (theta), log1m (theta))). The sum of the exponents is always one (and the log of that will be zero)! For every data point, you have to do: increment_log_prob (log_sum_exp (log (theta) + LP(y[i] | a_mu*, a_Sigma*), log1m (theta) + LP(y[i] | b_mu*, b_Sigma*) )). The parameters with asterisks represent the conditional distribution of y[i], given parameter a_mu, b_mu, a_Sigma, b_Sigma, and y[-i] (all data but y[i]). NB, these are not the full vector and matrix parameters that you define in the parameter block. See wikipedia on multivariate normal distributions, section conditional distribution of how to calculate that.

It's gonna be very ugly, I guarantee. I would strongly advise you try to find a simpler way to do this. You might want to consider fractional polynomials, or if you know the shape of the association between y and whatever the distance covariate is (I don't see it in your model), you could use a functional association (e.g. a general logistic function or whatnot).

I don't see why you would need theta to "have a sigmoid function", as theta simply represents a mixture weight. IMHO, theta seems fine as it is.

I've looked at L-BFGS-HMC. It is very good when there is not much curvature - i.e. the Hessian is fairly constant - but is not at all useful otherwise. It is quite easy to see why - the chains are in different parts of the space, spread out, so any approximate hessian is rather global, and doesn't reflect local behaviour. Imagine a strong banana, and the chains at different points in the banana.....

Maybe an adaptive approach which detects how much curvature there is, and uses L-BFGS-HMC when appropriate.....

My experience is that a bad approximate hessian can be worse than just a unit matrix or diagonal  Hessian.

> I thought I'd just share a few ideas for Stan. I'm still fairly new to the software, so I may misunderstand some of the features. Some of those ideas are likely to have been floated before, and I appreciate that the development team doesn't have unlimited resources.
>

>
> General
> ------------
>
> - Support for sparse covariance matrices / band diagonal Cholesky matrices would be swell for implementing some Gaussian processes, such as AR(p). Alternatively, supporting vector and array slicing could confer the same benefit.

Yup. That one's on our radar.  We do vector and matrix slicing and blocking, but
not general N-dimensional array operators.  Kronecker products also come up in
some of these settings.

> - Support for Daubechies wavelets and FFT is also useful to model large arrays with few coefficients.

No idea what this is, but it probably explains why someone
was asking us if we had an FFT function in Stan itself.

Discrete FFT's are pretty easy to compute and Eigen's library is
solid.  We're using it to compute autocorrelations in order to
estimate effective sample sizes.

I don't know how well auto-diffing Eigen's FFT algorithm would work.
Are there analytic gradients?

> - Some functions such as sqrt aren't yet vectorized.

Most functions aren't generalized to apply to vectors.  That's a
convenience issue as it won't be any faster in Stan to vectorize.

> Sampling
> ---------------
>
> - l-bfgs-hmc looks quite promising and seems much cheaper than Riemannian HMC.

See other response.

> - parallel tempering is big in molecular dynamics where finding where the mass of the distribution lies is half the battle. Any thoughts on it?

See Michael Betancourt's arXiv paper on thermodynamic sampling.
We plan to implement that sooner rather than later.  As soon as
I can generalize the model to split out the priors and likelihoods
(or bases and deltas as I believe Michael called them in the paper).

> Modeling language
> -------------------------------
>
> - Why not use name mangling to limit accidental collisions with C++ keywords?

This is a must-do that's on me to code up.  I've been meaning to
do it for ages.  It'll also prevent collisions with our own
built-in functions.

> - Parameters and generated quantities could be annotated to specify the sampler's behavior
> (@all: keep track of variable / @m[k]: keep track of the first k moments only / @category: keep track of the marginal categorical distribution of the parameter / @ignore: ignore)

We don't keep track of any moments directly (if by that you mean storing
X^2 as well as X --- they're easy to compute after the fact).

RStan lets you specify which variables to keep on the outside, but
we'll probably move to something more efficient with annotations like
you suggest in the model.  We're torn as to whether this is really part
of the model, so annotations seem reasonable.

>
> - If I'm not mistaken, upper and lower bounds only seem to apply during initialization and aren't enforced later on, unless T[] is used. The semantic is a little bit confusing as the bound is applied to the parameter's type, suggesting it's an intrinsic property. If it is only used for initialization, it should appear on the right hand side.

I'm not sure what you mean here.  If there are upper and lower bounds
declared on a parameter:

parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
}

then what happens is that we sample an underlying real variable that
is the logit-transform of theta (i.e., log(theta/(1-theta))).  Then
we inverse transform with inverse logit and apply the Jacobian to get
probabilities.  It happens every time the log probability function is
called.

Bounds on data and transformed data are validated once when the data's
read in for the data block and after the definitions in the transformed
data block.  Transformed parameters and generated quantities also both test
after their blocks have finished executing.

There are no constraints allowed on local variables because there's
no good way to keep them always satisfying their constraints.

>
> Python specific
> -------------------------
>
> - It would be very useful to be able to build a python representation of the model, before compilation, for debugging purposes. Beats "print".

You mean of the Stan program?  Stan isn't restricted
to graphical models like BUGS or JAGS.

There's an underlying abstract syntax tree that's
generated by the parser for the Stan language and then
used as the basis for C++ code generation.

> - Is there a way to pass a logger to the sampling method instead of having it write to stdout by default?

No idea.  Allen should know, though, so if he doesn't catch this note,
take it up again in an appropriately subjected message and I'm sure he'll
respond.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Expectations are means by definition.

There's an extensive literature on estimators that'll
tell you everything you need to know about point estimates
in terms of bias and variance (for instance, dividing
by (n-1) in a sample variance calculation gives you the
unbiased estimate, whereas dividing by n gives you the
maximum likelihood estimate).

Posterior means minimize expected square error, posterior medians
minimize expected absolute error, whereas posterior modes aren't
optimizing anything other than posterior density.  People use
all of them in various settings where it's too expensive to
calculate with the full posterior or where they want a single
summary statistic.

- Bob
