On Sep 11, 2014, at 11:43 AM, Arthur B. <arthur....@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Wednesday, September 10, 2014 1:28:47 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> Agreed.  Vectorizing everything's on our to-do list.
>
>
> Wait, that  .size() function, though mentioned in the documentation on page 213 - isn't actually there...

No idea how that creeped in.  I'm supposed to be making
sure all these functions parse!  There's a size() function
for arrays and then rows() and columns() for matrices and
vectors.  But nothing with syntax like .size()!

> I can't do  inv_logit( v )

Not yet.

> I can't do 1 /. (1 + exp( -v ))  ( can't divide scalar by vector )

You should be able to do this.

> I can't do size( v ) because size only applies to arrays.

cols(v) is what you want if v is a column vector.

We should probably extend size() to vectors (and even to
matrices, where size is (M x N) --- Eigen lets you index
matrices in column-major order with a single index, which
might also be convenient in places in Stan).

> I can do exp(-log(1+exp(-v))) but that's such a waste of computation !
> I can pass a length parameter known at compile time, but it's clunky
> Or I can convert to an array first, but I don't know what the overhead is on that...z

Not much overhead converting to an array.  The bigger problem is
the clutter and lack of readability in the model.   Most of Stan's time,
either for optimization or sampling, is  spent in autodiff calculating
gradients.

> Am I missing another way?

But you can use the logit-parameterized log
probability functions, like bernoulli_logit and
binomial_logit, and equivalently categorical_logit.  And
you can append _log to that to get the log probability
function if you need it in a mixture model or something.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Question on Bayesian Cognitive Modeling code
messages.subject_clean: Question on Bayesian Cognitive Modeling code
messages.body_plain:
For Stan, each chain is split in half when the R-hat statistic is calculated. This allows it to be calculated (technically) when there is only one chain to split and in general is better at catching chains that drift in similar ways. The Stan manual mentions this in the chapter on MCMC. Still, I wouldn't run just one chain.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] interpretation of traceplot
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] interpretation of traceplot
messages.body_plain:
The usual explanation is that you're getting into portions of the posterior
with different curvature that are hard to get out of once you get into
them.  This isn't a bug --- it's just a consequence of the fact that HMC
and NUTS satisfy detailed balance.

The reason it's hard to step out is usually that adaptation has
created too large a step size.  So what you can try to do is lower
the step size.  The easiest way to do this is to up the target
acceptance rate (delta).

- Bob

On Sep 13, 2014, at 8:31 PM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:

> It's also in the text and footnote in BDA3, where the splitting is mentioned. I've e-mailed Dr. Plummer asking if he implements the change in coda. FWIW, I think it's still based on the original Gelman and Rubin paper.

Martyn said he was going to update Coda to use the split R-hat metric.

And yes, it's still based on the original R-hat --- the only difference
is that each chain's split in two to diagnose a bunch of chains all slowly
drifting in the same direction.  Or to measure one long chain against
itself, though as Ben said, it's not what we'd recommend except during model
debugging.  (The case of models like mixtures that don't identify parameters
is an argument for just running one long chain.)

- Bob

>
> Avi
>
> On Saturday, September 13, 2014 9:35:03 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> For Stan, each chain is split in half when the R-hat statistic is calculated. This allows it to be calculated (technically) when there is only one chain to split and in general is better at catching chains that drift in similar ways. The Stan manual mentions this in the chapter on MCMC. Still, I wouldn't run just one chain.
>
> Ben
>

> thanks,
>
> Shravan

messages.body_plain:
We want to run multiple chains to diagnose convergence better.
Ironically, evaluating R-hat on non-identified parameters like
mixture components is what's difficult!

For most posterior inferences, the unidentified components are
going to be marginalized out anyway.  Should we just not bother
monitoring  convergence on the mixture component parameters?

I know this brings up how we improve global convergence monitoring.
Would that somehow help with mixture components?

In other cases than mixtures, there really shouldn't be unidentified parameters
in a proper model --- we want to identify so that we can adapt and mix
well without devolving into long random walks in the unconstrained space.

The mixture case is the one we don't seem to be
able to parameterize away due to the arguments you made about
correlation of parameters and their interaction in things like ordering.
For instance, you might identify two mixture components with mu1 and
mu2 having posterior 90% intervals (-1,1) and (0,2) or something like
that.  But if you use an ordered vector, you wind up with mu1 < mu2 in
all iterations.

- Bob

But that's the problem --- how do we monitor convergence of
the parameters involved in the mixture components?

p(y | lambda, mu1, sigma1, mu2, sigma2)

   = lambda * normal(y|mu1,sigma1)

     + (1 - lambda) * normal(y|mu2,sigma2)

(mu1,sigma1) and (mu2,sigma2) are going to be swappable.  And if
there's a narrow enough trough between the modes, you might even
swap within a single chain.

- Bob

just constrain mu1 < mu2 because even if

messages.body_plain:
To be completely clear — chains properly sampling the entirety of a multimodal
distribution will yield an Rhat of 1.  The problem here is when we have samplers
that cannot explore modes efficiently.

If the modes are not meaningful because of, for example, label switching degeneracies
then the easy answer is to just find a transformed parameter that doesn’t depend
on the labels and compute Rhat from that.  But if the modes are meaningful then
we would want Rhat to diagnose this as a problem because a chain that can’t
sample from both modes at once will have biased inferences.

Breaking degeneracies through modeling may work, but it will be delicate.  In the
mixture of Gaussians example ordering will work only if | mu1 - mu2 | >> 0 so that
the overlap Bob mentions is inconsequential.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Current state of ODE solvers?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Current state of ODE solvers?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gustaf,

If you're talking about Gillespie, that implies you're interested in stochastic simulation, which will be outside the scope of what they're building for Stan.

If I understand it properly, the use case for the Stan ODE solver is a deterministic system with observation error—the underlying dynamics are not stochastic, and there's no process error, so the likelihood comes just from the observation model atop the ODE dynamics. Stan should then let you infer the posterior distribution over parameters governing both the system dynamics as well as the observation model.

If you know you need process noise, you'll have to look elsewhere, e.g., particle filter methods such as the MIF algorithm implemented here:

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pomp/index.html

Under MIF, you can generate simulations from stochastic ODEs or Gillespie or anything you like, but the computational cost is very high, because you're effectively integrating over all possible stochastic realizations of the model. (I imagine there are fully Bayesian particle filter-style methods out there as well.)

But you're going to want to start without process noise anyway, and Stan 2.5 should make that easy.

Ed

messages.subject: Feedback on speeding up slow, hierarchical model of test kinetics
messages.subject_clean: Feedback on speeding up slow, hierarchical model of test kinetics
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I’m trying to figure out ways of making my (relatively complex but not obscenely so) model run better, and would greatly appreciate any help in that regard! I’m running Stan 2.4.0 via Rstan, using R 3.1.1 on OSX10.9.4, on a Macbook Pro 2ghz/16b RAM.

 The (hierarchical) model has 1700 parameters in total  and 500 observations . It  is currently taking approximately 8hours per chain (run in parallel, so 8hrs total) for 5k iterations, but with runs varying in time from 4-8hours per chain. At that point, some parameters have ”converged”, with Rhat of  around 1, but _lp has an Rhat of 1.4, and 100/1700 parameters have Rhats of 2-4.
The model fit to the data is also kinda rubbish, but I suspect that’s down to some sillyness of my own with regards to the choice of priors.

I tried looking at get_sampler_params: one of four chains seems to converge to a region with a small number of leapfrogs after ~3000 iterations (2^3 tree depth, 3-5 jumps); the other three are stuck around 2000.

I’ve attached my model code. This is an attempt to replicate a model published in Stats in Medicine in 2009 (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sim.3592/abstract ) - I'm using their data, but only a third of the observations, to speed things up. Their model was implemented in WinBugs, and apparently ran relatively quickly.

Briefly, it's modelling three IG levels per patient, each patient being measured several times. The development of IG levels over time is described by a four-parameter function, with parameters X.star,S,a,D. This function is continuous, but have different behaviour if t<D or t>D, and so I'm using an if... else clause - I suspect this is a problem, but don't know how to go about it .

Again, any feedback would be much appreciated!

Best,
Gustaf

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Gustaf.  This is an unusual model in that you have a parameter with a prior scaled to 0.0001.  This might make sense in your example but in general we recommend scaling things so that parameters are of order of magnitude 1.  Regarding the discontinuity: it might be a good idea to try a fully continuous model and see how it goes.  Then if it goes fast, you’ll know that the problem is the discontinuity and you can think of ways of speeding things up (for example, making the model itself a bit more continuous, which, following the principle of the Folk Theorem, might even make it a better model) and if the continuous model is slow then you can continue to strip down the model until it runs fast, so you can figure out where the problem is.

Also you could try carefully choosing starting points.  This can make a difference, especially if some chains are going really slow.

Andrew

messages.body_plain:
You want to use quad_form_diag instead of the diag_matrix construction.
It should be much more efficient.  But the big speedup would be in
going to a cholesky factor parameterization rather than a covariance
matrix one.

Is that cauchy(0,0.0001) really meant to be the other way around and
be very diffuse?  Stan uses scale parameters (1/precision^2) for distributions,
not precisions.

You could probably scrunch all those theta2IgLogmu priors into
a single vectorized call, with

  to_vector(theta2IgLogmu[i]) ~ cauchy(0, 0.1);

Also, our multi_normal is now vectorized and generalized from column
vectors to also work on row vectors.  So you shouldn't need the to_vector
on these:

  for(i in 1:I){
    ...
    for(n in 1:N){
      to_vector(row(theta1IgLogmu[n],i))~multi_normal(to_vector(row(theta2IgLogmu,i)),igCov[i]);
    }
  }

To start, row(x,i) is longhand for x[i].  And you don't need the to_vector any more,
so this is all just:

  for(i in 1:I){
    ...
    for(n in 1:N){
      theta1IgLogmu[n,i] ~ multi_normal(theta2IgLogmu[i] ,igCov[i]);
    }
  }

But what you really want to do for speed is transpose theta1IgLogmu by defining
theta1IgLogmu_t such that you can write the above as:

  for(i in 1:I){
    ...
    theta1IgLogmu_t[i] ~ multi_normal(theta2IgLogmu[i] ,igCov[i]);
  }

You have to declare thetaIgLogMu_t as

  vector[K] thetaIgLogMu_t[I,N];

and then use it so that

  theta1IgLogmu_t[i,n,k] = theta1IgLogmu[n,i,k]

and so that theta1IgLogmu_t[i] is an array of vectors, which is what
you need in the argument position to vectorize.

There's a chapter in the manual explaining efficiency issues of
arrays vs. vectors/matrices.

Any of the variables in transformed parameters you don't want to
save can be declared as locals in the model block (or in the transformed
parameters block if you need them later in the transformed param block
but not in the model).

You might also find it helpful to declare variables to be constrained
to be positive so you don't have to do an exp() transform, but then
I see you're creating a log multinormal distribution the theta1IgLogmu, so
that probably won't help.  You should see if everything's stable and you're
not getting any rejections during iterations due to arithmetic issues
(shows up in CmdStan as divergences in the print of parameters --- I'm sure
you can fish it out somehow in PyStan or RStan, too).

This:

  omegaCorr ~ lkj_corr(1);  /////prior for the within-measurement correlation

is implicit because it's uniform on correlation matrices.  If you really
want that, you can just remove the sampling statement.  All variables are
implicitly uniform on values satisfying their constraints.

This stuff you want to vectorize:

for(i in 1:I){
    tau[i] ~ cauchy(0,0.0001); ///prior for the within-measurement scale
    igTau[i]~cauchy(0,0.1);  ///prior for the within-parameter scale
    igCorr[i]~lkj_corr(1.5);

to just

  tau ~ cauchy(0, 1e-4);
  igTau ~ cauchy(0,1e-1);
  for (i in 1:I)
    igCorr[i] ~ lkj_corr(1.5);

It's just as efficient, if not more so, to put each variable in its
own loop.  It's better for memory locality and loops themselves are
usually pretty much free (that is, it's very unlike R or Python
in terms of what's costly).

That should speed everything up a lot in terms of how long it takes
each iteration.  But it won't help convergence (unless there's an issue
with the priors).  Tightening priors can help, as can initializing
at a reasonable starting point if convergence is taking a long time.

If you have the WinBUGS code and are worried you've translated it
wrong, we'd be happy to look at pieces.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A few ideas for future versions...
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] A few ideas for future versions...
messages.body_plain:
Here's another potentially interesting feature.

Computing the likelihood, let alone the gradient, can be quite expensive in large datasets. Linear regression models on large datasets have benefited greatly from stochastic gradient descent. It turns out something similar can be achieved in MCMC. Instead of computing the likelihood of an entire i.i.d sample, this likelihood can be approximated by using a small, random, subsample.

Using the generalized poisson estimator introduced in Fearnhead, Papaspiliopoulos and Roberts [1], a subset of the data can be used as an unbiased estimate of the log likelihood and provide and unbiased acceptance / rejection step.

Quiroz, Villani, and Kohn [2] suggest doing a simple convexity adjustment by assuming normality of the log likelihood distribution across the sample, and Barnet, Doucet, and Holmes [3] seem to take another approach altogether, but with the same goal of using a subsample.

In theory, this should translate to an HMC sampler, though it might decrease the acceptance rate.

[1] http://arxiv.org/pdf/0710.4245.pdf
[2] http://arxiv.org/pdf/1404.4178v1.pdf
[3] http://jmlr.org/proceedings/papers/v32/bardenet14.pdf

as you would need to scale something like an IRT model or
really any model with random effects that grow with the data.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
While we're at it, there's also the crossentropy method.

If you have a good analytical approximation of your posterior for which maximum likelihood is tractable, you can alternate between importance sampling, and fitting it to the drawn samples.

It has the advantage that it's a global approach, it has the disadvantage that, well, the posterior is probably not well approximated by anything tractable.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Now that we have functions and ODE's are not far behind, this feature (assigning to segments or slices of vectors, matrices or arrays) seems like it deserves even higher priority. I keep encountering situations where I want to define functions that return vectors, matrices or arrays. Often those functions are to be applied repeatedly but with varying dimensions of the return value. A typical example would a function to calculate a vector of predicted drug concentrations over multiple observation times for each individual patient in a clinical trial. More often than not the patients differ w.r.t. the number and timing of observations. So far I haven't figured out any good kluges to get around this other than to just make functions that return scalar values and do the calculations separately for each observation time.

Just a friendly nudge....

Thanks,
Bill

Yes, definitely something we should do.  Not to mention the
more ambitious problem of allowing general R/MATLAB-style
slicing syntax (e.g, a[,2:3,5] <- b[6:7,8]).

As much as I'd like to enrich the language, I don't think
this one's even in the top hundred on our to-do list (not
that we're that organized).  This one's hard to pass off to
someone else because it changes the notion of lvalue and
rvalue in the language.  There's an example for assigning to
rows of matrices, but that's it.  So it wouldn't be impossible
for someone outside the core dev team to take it on, it's
more likely something I'll have to do personally.

It would be great if someone wants to volunteer to help with
parsing and code gen.  The real bottleneck now is that I'm
about the only one comfortable with that part of the code.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Thierry,

Like you, I am looking forward to implementation of ODE solvers in Stan. I plan to take advantage of them to construct Stan functions for PKPD modeling that can handle complicated event histories in a manner similar to NONMEM's NMTRAN and PREDPP components. A stiff ODE solver, or even better a solver that automatically adapts between solvers for non-stiff and stiff ODE's like LSODA, would be great.

Until then one option is the BUGSModelLibrary package (https://code.google.com/p/bugsmodellibrary/) for WinBUGS 1.4.3. It gives the user a choice between multiple solvers including LSODA. The tradeoffs will be (possibly) more efficient ODE solving but less efficient sampling with WinBUGS/BUGSModelLibrary versus Stan with the non-stiff solver. It might be worth trying both options and selecting the one that performs best for your particular problem.

Regards,
Bill

messages.subject: Re: STIFF ODE solver in STAN
messages.subject_clean: STIFF ODE solver in STAN
messages.body_plain:
A 200-fold difference could mean a slowdown of 200-fold.
It has to take a step size controlled by the fastest moving
variable.

How many parameters do you have there?

In Stan, the dimension of the solver (i.e., integrator) used is

   N = (1 + num_params) * state_dimension

because we add to the original state y, the sensitivities d.state/d.param,
which is is a um_params * state_dimension matrix.

We need d.state/d.param in order to compute derivatives of
the solutions w.r.t. the parameters in order to use HMC.

For stiff systems, we then need to compute an N*N Jacobian.
So the slowdown's essentially going to be a constant * N-fold,
where the constant is the extra cost to evaluate with reverse-mode
nested in forward-mode autodiff compared to with just reverse-mode;
so maybe another factor of 2--4.

We're working on a new autodiff implementation that'll be much more
efficient at Hessians and Jacobians (and third-order calculations).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

I have 15 parameters and 16 states, so according to your explanation N will be high and the slowdown quite significant.
I think it's worth trying and compare the results with WinBUGS/BUGSModelLibrary (that has the LSODA solver) like Bill suggested.

Regards,
Thierry

Le mercredi 17 septembre 2014 18:11:52 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> A 200-fold difference could mean a slowdown of 200-fold.
> It has to take a step size controlled by the fastest moving
> variable.
>
> How many parameters do you have there?
>
> In Stan, the dimension of the solver (i.e., integrator) used is
>
>    N = (1 + num_params) * state_dimension
>
> because we add to the original state y, the sensitivities d.state/d.param,
> which is is a um_params * state_dimension matrix.
>
> We need d.state/d.param in order to compute derivatives of
> the solutions w.r.t. the parameters in order to use HMC.
>
> For stiff systems, we then need to compute an N*N Jacobian.
> So the slowdown's essentially going to be a constant * N-fold,
> where the constant is the extra cost to evaluate with reverse-mode
> nested in forward-mode autodiff compared to with just reverse-mode;
> so maybe another factor of 2--4.
>
> We're working on a new autodiff implementation that'll be much more
> efficient at Hessians and Jacobians (and third-order calculations).
>
> - Bob
>
> On Sep 17, 2014, at 10:18 AM, Wendling, Thierry <thierry....@novartis.com> wrote:
>
> > Dear Andrew and Bob,
> >
> > Thanks for your quick feedback.
> >
> > Unfortunately I'm not very familiar with the algorithm used in LSODA (other users might help here) but my understanding is that yes, it does calculate a Jacobian.
> >
> > I will try the solver of the next Stan version, although it might struggle for this particular problem given the dimension of my model (16 ODEs) and the high difference between the time constant of some compartments (>200-fold).
> >
> > Regards,
> > Thierry
> >
> > -----Original Message-----
> > From: Bob Carpenter [mailto:ca...@alias-i.com]
> > Sent: Mittwoch, 17. September 2014 05:38
> > To: Andrew Gelman
> > Cc: Wendling, Thierry; stan-...@googlegroups.com; Daniel Lee
> > Subject: Re: STIFF ODE solver in STAN
> >
> > Yes, we eventually plan to implement stiff solvers in Stan.
> > It might be a while, though, as in six to twelve months.
> >
> > Do you know how LSODA deals with stiffness?  That is, does it calculate a Jacobian, and if so, how?
> >
> > Depending on what your model is, you could use MCSim, written by Frederic Bois, who's also helping us with Stan's ODE solvers.
> > I don't know if it'll support the kind of model you want, but it looks pretty flexible.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > On Sep 16, 2014, at 11:23 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >
> >> Hi, Thierry.  I'm cc-ing Bob Carpenter and Daniel Lee, who are implementing the ODE solvers, and also cc-ing the stan-users list since others should be interested in this.  The short answer is that I think you should try the Stan ode solver (which we are planning to introduce in a near-future Stan version).  It's hard for me to say ahead of time how well it will work on a particular example, but I will say that it will typically run better if the starting points are chosen carefully.

Same problem.  Stan code is executed in order and variables
must be defined before they are used.

It looks like you also have an indexing problem.

model {
  ...
  matrix[nsites,nspecies] Mu;
  ...
  for(species in 1:nspecies) {
    for(k in 1:K) {
      Betaraw[species,k] ~ normal(muraw[k], tau[k]);
    }
  }

  for (sites in 1:nsites) {
    for (species in 1:nspecies) {
      Mu[species, sites] <- dot_product(Betaraw[species], X[sites]);
      Z[sites] ~ multi_normal(Mu[sites], Tau);

1.  You need to define the relevant parts of Mu before you use it.
You haven't, which is why you're getting NaN errors.

2.  The second problem is that you use Mu[sites], which is indexed
the wrong way around compared to how Mu[species,sites] is defined.
Mu[sites] is the row with index sites out of Mu.  You can extract
the column with col(Mu,sites).

But what you really want to do is just set up your Betaraw and
X appropriately so that you can do a matrix product and then
vectorize multi_normal.  We can help you with that if you get the
basic model working first.  Otherwise, I'd just be guessing.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: STIFF ODE solver in STAN
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: STIFF ODE solver in STAN
messages.body_plain:
Our case is a bit special because we need the sensitivities
(derivatives of state w.r.t. parameters and initial state)
calculated along with the basic system solution.  This
coupled system has a lot of structure, as Michael Betancourt's
been exploring.  It turns out the Jacobian of the coupled
system is going to have a great deal of structure we can
exploit.

Systems like LSODA take the system as a whole, figure
out the Jacobians with finite diffs when they need to,
and try to do something clever with sparseness.  You can
also plug in your own Jacobian function, which is what I
think we'll have to do in the end (though we'll probably try
just letting their built-ins loose and see how they do).
LSODA itself allows for banded Jacobians, which may turn out to
be sufficient to control the kinds of stiffness we care about.

For Stan 2.5, it'll just be Boost's Runge-Kutta implementation
for non-stiff system.

Hopefully in the next six to nine months we'll be able to
roll out something more robust to stiffness that's not too
onerous computationally.

And thanks to everyone for all the input --- we really appreciate
it!

- Bob

On Sep 18, 2014, at 5:07 AM, Thierry Wendling <thierry....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Bob,
>
> I have 15 parameters and 16 states, so according to your explanation N will be high and the slowdown quite significant.
> I think it's worth trying and compare the results with WinBUGS/BUGSModelLibrary (that has the LSODA solver) like Bill suggested.
>
> Regards,
> Thierry
>
> Le mercredi 17 septembre 2014 18:11:52 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> A 200-fold difference could mean a slowdown of 200-fold.
> It has to take a step size controlled by the fastest moving
> variable.
>
> How many parameters do you have there?
>
> In Stan, the dimension of the solver (i.e., integrator) used is
>
>    N = (1 + num_params) * state_dimension
>
> because we add to the original state y, the sensitivities d.state/d.param,
> which is is a um_params * state_dimension matrix.
>
> We need d.state/d.param in order to compute derivatives of
> the solutions w.r.t. the parameters in order to use HMC.
>
> For stiff systems, we then need to compute an N*N Jacobian.
> So the slowdown's essentially going to be a constant * N-fold,
> where the constant is the extra cost to evaluate with reverse-mode
> nested in forward-mode autodiff compared to with just reverse-mode;
> so maybe another factor of 2--4.
>
> We're working on a new autodiff implementation that'll be much more
> efficient at Hessians and Jacobians (and third-order calculations).
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am trying to get an understanding of the performance of Stan in terms of both runtime and chain mixing. I ran the standard school ranking problem from BUGS examples, http://www.openbugs.net/Examples/Schools.html. I used the model file and data file from

jags: http://www.openbugs.net/Examples/Schools.html
stan: https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/master/bugs_examples/vol2/schools

However, I am surprised to find that jags finishes 1000 warm up and 1000 iterations in 10 seconds, while Stan takes 1200 seconds. Both for one chain.

I am running on windows 8 with a 2.4GHz Intel i5 processor and 8G memory.

I further profile the performance using Intel VTune, and I am surprised (again) to find that Stan executes 30 times the floating point operations as Jags (partially explains why it's slow). Is that because Stan uses a different algorithm (HMC) from Jags? Or is there any other reasons?

I am also getting a lot of warnings from running Stan. Is that the issue?

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter[61]  is 0:0, but must be > 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

Thanks very much!
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

When comparing performance, you really want to look at the number of effective samples per second. The error message is only an indicator of a Metropolis rejection, which, as it says, is fine if it occurs sporadically. As I remember it, the schools example doesn't throw these rejections all the time, but just during initialization / warmup.

You will see this error very often (but not exclusively so) when the support of one of your parameters (declared in the parameter block) extends beyond its prior. messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

This is described in the Stan manual on page 5 in the subsection called "Convergence Monitoring and Effective Sample Size." I think the high level picture is described well enough in the manual, BDA3, and across this users list where I don't think I'd be adding anything useful.

Perhaps explaining what you need to do will help:
1. Run Stan and JAGS.
2. Calculate the runtime.
3. Calculate the number of effective samples. For Stan, if you're running in RStan or PyStan, the display of the fit object will contain the number of effective samples. If you're using CmdStan, bin/print will print the number of effective samples. For JAGS, after you get the samples, you can run RStan's monitor() function to calculate the number of effective samples.
4. Compare the quantity (runtime / effective samples) for Stan and JAGS.

There is an additional, necessary step between 1 & 2. You'll have to verify that the models are the same and the inferences are the same. The hard part is making sure the Stan program matches the JAGS program including all parts of the joint posterior. Then you'll have to verify that the inferences are the same for all parameters in the model. The comparison is worthless if one program or both are not actually getting the "right" answer.

Hope that helps.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
messages.body_plain:
1.  Yes, measure n_eff/second --- both the Coda output for
JAGS and the Stan output for Stan will give you n_eff in
their output.

2.  How are you running Stan?  Do you have all the optimization
turned on?  Are both systems being given the same starting point?
Do both systems converge (R-hat below 1.05 for all parameters)?

3.  The messages are coming from the exp() expression in this:

  exp(-.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)

underflowing.  If this evaluates to less than -800 or so, the
exp() underflows to 0.  So one question to ask is whether both
systems, JAGS and BUGS, are getting appropriately into the tails.
If this is happening just during warmup, I wouldn't worry about it.

Was that min.var and max.var somehow being used in the JAGS
model?

4.  This model's probably not well identified.  phi looks particularly
bad in the BUGS fit (posterior mean -.0026 and posterior sd 0.0029).
(this is being multipled by a factor of order (-30,30) and then exponentiated).
The posteriors for the coefficients beta don't look very well identified, either.

The whole model is fitting a quadratic function of LRT[p] with hierarchical
parameters.   The coefficients don't look very well identiied.
It'd be useful to see if the Stan posterior intervals match those
of JAGS.

I'd suggest tightening up those normal(0,100) priors to something
reasonable for the expected coefficient sizes, which in the posterior are
all less than 1.  These are just
holdervers from the super-diffuse dnorm(0,0.0001) priors from the BUGS
models.

5.  There are a lot of ways to optimize this very out-of-date
Stan code.  The biggest and simplest speedup would be to
replace this:

  for (m in 1:M) alpha[m] ~ multi_normal(gamma, Sigma);

with

  alpha ~ multi_normal(gamma, Sigma);

But really we want to parameterize this all in terms of Cholesky
factors.  We don't have a good way to do this with inverse Wisharts,
yet.  We'd recommend using the LKJ priors instead (which is why they're
coded more efficiently).  They're easier to parameterize to concentrate
mass around the unit correlation matrix and then independently scale.

The general statement of this

  gamma ~ multi_normal(gamma_mu, gamma_Sigma);

isn't necessary when gamma_Sigma is set to a diagonal matrix.
This should be replaced with:

   gamma ~ normal(0,10);

The BUGS model let you specify gamma_mu and gamma_Sigma as data,
then passed in a zero vector for gamma_mu and a scaled unit
matrix for gamma_Sigma.

6.  There are also alternative parameterizations.  Is there a multivariate
version of the Matt trick out there?

7.  I think we should be computing min.var and max.var.
We could do that a little less hardcoded, I think.

Anyway, the bottom line here is that the Schools model as coded
isn't a good indication of what Stan can do :-)  We should fix
this ourselves so it's a better example.

- Bob

One question I have is whether we should stick to exactly
the same model as in JAGS/BUGS?

Yes, this looks like a case where the model's not identified
properly.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
messages.body_plain:
First a theory question --- the posterior shows lp__ ranging
from -180 to -70 --- is that much range indicative of a problem?

I wrote two new versions of the BUGS vol2/schools example.

I'm appending the models.  If anyone has any optimization suggestions
or reparameterization suggestions, let me know and I can try them out.

1.  Just a more efficient version of the same model.  I
tightened the priors a bit, and used a vectorized form
of multi_normal on the precision scale.

2.  Rewritten with LKJ priors using a correlation matrix
plus scale parameterization.

In both instances, rejection warnings arise during the first
few warmup iterations from the scale going to 0 in:

  Y ~ normal(Ymu,  exp(-0.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)));

It's taking a tree depth of 7 or 8 on average, going out to 11
quite often.  So we should probably even deepen the
tree depth here to see if we're getting the right fit.

R-hat is good with four chains.  The second model takes about
550 seconds for 1000 warmup iterations and 200 seconds for 1000 sampling
iterations.  Effective sample sizes with four chains (4000 saved
draws) range from 75 or so for the hierarchical scale to 4000
for theta and phi.  That's a pretty lousy 3 seconds/effective sample
after warmup or so.

The sign of phi isn't identified, with a 95% interval of
(-0.008, 0.003).  LRT ranges between [-35,35] or so, and then
it's all inside that exp(-0.5 * ...).  theta is around 0.6.

The BUGS report in their manual is for 10K runs and our estimates
match reasonably well --- they only provide posterior
summaries for some of the regression coefficients, not the priors,
which are what have low effective sample sizes with Stan.

The above tests were with RStan 2.4.

- Bob

Optimized a bit
----------------

/**
 * Schools: ranking school examination results
 * http://www.openbugs.info/Examples/Schools.html
 */
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> M;
  vector[N] LRT;
  int school[N];
  int School_denom[N, 3];
  int School_gender[N, 2];
  int VR[N, 2];
  real Y[N];
  int Gender[N];
  cov_matrix[3] R;
}
parameters {
  real beta[8];
  real<lower=0> theta;
  real phi;
  vector[3] alpha[M];
  vector[3] gamma;
  cov_matrix[3] Omega;
}
model {
  real Ymu[N];
  for(p in 1:N)
    Ymu[p] <- alpha[school[p],1]
      + alpha[school[p],2] * LRT[p]
      + alpha[school[p],3] * VR[p,1]
      + beta[1] * LRT[p] * LRT[p]
      + beta[2] * VR[p,2]
      + beta[3] * Gender[p]
      + beta[4] * School_gender[p,1]
      + beta[5] * School_gender[p,2]
      + beta[6] * School_denom[p,1]
      + beta[7] * School_denom[p,2]
      + beta[8] * School_denom[p,3];

  Y ~ normal(Ymu,  theta); // exp(-0.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)));

  # Priors for fixed effects:
  beta ~ normal(0, 5);

Modified with LKJ priors and cholesky factors

/**
 * Schools: ranking school examination results
 * http://www.openbugs.info/Examples/Schools.html
 */
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> M;
  vector[N] LRT;
  int school[N];
  int School_denom[N, 3];
  int School_gender[N, 2];
  int VR[N, 2];
  real Y[N];
  int Gender[N];
  cov_matrix[3] R;
}
parameters {
  real beta[8];
  real theta;
  real phi;
  vector[3] alpha[M];
  vector[3] gamma;
  cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
  vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;
}
model {
  real Ymu[N];
  for(p in 1:N)
    Ymu[p] <- alpha[school[p],1]
      + alpha[school[p],2] * LRT[p]
      + alpha[school[p],3] * VR[p,1]
      + beta[1] * LRT[p] * LRT[p]
      + beta[2] * VR[p,2]
      + beta[3] * Gender[p]
      + beta[4] * School_gender[p,1]
      + beta[5] * School_gender[p,2]
      + beta[6] * School_denom[p,1]
      + beta[7] * School_denom[p,2]
      + beta[8] * School_denom[p,3];

  Y ~ normal(Ymu,  exp(-0.5 * (theta + phi * LRT)));

  # Priors for fixed effects:
  beta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  theta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  phi ~ normal(0, 0.1);

  # Priors for random coefficients:
  alpha ~ multi_normal_cholesky(gamma, diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma));

  # Hyper-priors:
  gamma ~ normal(0, 5);
  sigma_Sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  L_Sigma ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(3);
}

- Bob

On Sunday, September 21, 2014 12:04:11 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'm appending the models.  If anyone has any optimization suggestions
> or reparameterization suggestions, let me know and I can try them out.

General rule: Do not use any of the variants of multi_normal when the left-hand side is a parameter.

If there is a law in your country that you have to use the inverse Wishart prior for the covariance matrix of multivariate normal coefficients, integrate the evil covariance matrix out:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-Wishart_distribution#Conjugate_distribution

and write the prior on the coefficients in terms of the inverse scale matrix and degrees of freedom. HMC has difficulty sampling inverse Wishart covariance matrices, so integrating it out helps numerically. But it is still a bad prior theoretically, and the Schools2.stan attachment, still yields bad performance if you run enough chains (i.e. 4 is too few).

Otherwise, decompose the covariance matrix into standard deviations and a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix but do not use multi_normal_cholesky. If the multivariate distribution is within the elliptical family and the thing is unknown, always utilize the stochastic representation with i.i.d. standard normal primitives. Schools3.stan can be slower in walltime but is much better at effective sample size.

Ben

On Monday, September 22, 2014 7:55:55 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> This should become part of the FAQ. Very important piece of information. If possible, then it would be really nice to have this trick done directly behind the scenes if applicable.
>
> May I ask why the "stochastic" representation is so much better when the LHS are parameters? Any theoretical insights here?

I guess we could write an elliptical_transformation() function that would do the math slightly more quickly. But you would still have to reparameterize the model to have the right things in the parameters block, so it can't be fully automated.

With NUTS, you always want the parameters to have a scale near 1 and be uncorrelated with other parameters. If you are using a

beta[j] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);

hierarchical prior, then beta[j] depends on mu and even worse on Sigma. In particular, for a nearly singular proposal for Sigma, beta[j] has to be nearly linearly dependent (i.e. one of its elements is nearly fixed, given the other elements).

But if you make beta[j] a transformed parameter with

beta[j] <- mu + L * z[j];

then all the elements of z are (a priori) unit-scaled, mutually independent, and independent of L. It really is the multivariate version of the Matt trick with a Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix serving the role of the standard deviation of a scalar. If L gets nearly-singular, then the last element of z[j] is not well-identified by the data but has a standard normal prior in the model block.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

So I'm working on this model I have with censored-lognormal hidden
parameters. Now, I don't actually care about those hidden parameters
so I can integrate them out, replacing expressions such as

 gap_self ~ lognormal(gap_self_mean, gap_self_stdv) T[timepos[n] -
prevtimes[k],];

with

 increment_log_prob(lognormal_ccdf_log(timepos[n] - prevtimes[k],
gap_self_mean, gap_self_stdv));

and thus avoiding having to sample the parameters that create "gap_self".

The full models are here:
* Explicit sampling: <http://tinyurl.com/k2pfcmq>
* Integrating out: <http://tinyurl.com/kfodkff>
* And the toy data: <http://tinyurl.com/kohe2xd> for which the true
parameters are gap_self_mean = 1.23, gap_self_stdv = 0.654.

These models look equivalent to me, but the explicit version
repeatedly gets a good estimate of my test data true parameters, while
the integrating-out version is worse. It should be better, surely,
since it samples a much smaller parameter space. Both approaches get
good Rhat and Neff.

Is there something I've missed in my conversion? Is there any reason
to expect explicit sampling to work better?

Thanks
Dan

messages.body_plain:
Here's what I wrote to stan-dev on the issue of
adding function support for the Ben trick (aka multivariate
non-centered parameterization).

As Ben points out, the obstacle to full automation is that we
don't have a way to write a function that injects parameters and
transformed parameters.

On the other hand, we could forego the transformed parameters
and just have the user declare the raw parameters, then we
could make the transformed parameters local in the function,
and the function could apply the normal(0,1) prior to the raw
parameters.  The downside is that it hides the transformed
parameters, which can be the estimands of interest, as in
the BUGS vol2 schools model.

We could also consider some notion of program transform behind
the scenes.  It's tricky figuring out how to apply it.
For instance, we might look for

  alpha ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma)

where alpha is a parameter and swap out for non-centered.
Then we can look at where Sigma is a parameter and swap out
for a Cholesky factor (assuming we have the priors that were
used for Sigma).

- Bob

> From: Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>
> Subject: Re: [stan-dev] Fwd: [stan-users] schools ranking problem using Stan and JAGS
> Date: September 21, 2014 at 3:39:22 PM EDT
> To: stan...@googlegroups.com

> Brilliant!  Works like a charm.  This is much better
> converging and much better mixing once converged.  Roughly
> 1 effective sample every 1--3 draws across all parameters.
>
> I'll try to make this standard operating procedure.
>
> It's a little less intensive on the multiplies with
>
>  diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma) * z
>
> instead of
>
>  diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma * z)
>
> because they are (3 x 1), (3 x 3) and (3 x M) respectively.
> Eigen's clever enough to figure this all out on its own
> using expression templates, but Stan's not that clever.
>
> It would be more efficient with a diag_pre_multiply_lower_tri()
> function.  In fact, we pretty much need a whole bunch of
> specializations of matrix ops for:
>
>    diagonal matrices (as vectors)
>    symmetric matrices
>    lower-triangular (upper-triangular) matrices
>    symmetric, positive definite matrices
>    correlation matrices ?
>
> This is a nice modular project someone could take on a little
> bit at a time that'd make a big difference in multivariate modeling
> speed.
>
> Here's the full Ben trick, isolated for inspection:
>
>  parameters {
>    matrix[3,M] z;

>    vector[3] gamma;
>    cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
>    vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;

>    ...
>  transformed parameters {
>     matrix[M,3] alpha;
>     alpha <- transpose(rep_matrix(gamma,M)
>                        + diag_pre_multiply(sigma_Sigma, L_Sigma) * z);
>  }
>  model {
>    to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
>
>
> which produces the equivalent of
>
>
>  parameters {

>    vector[3] gamma;
>    cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Sigma;
>    vector<lower=0>[3] sigma_Sigma;

>    matrix[M,3] alpha;
>    ...
>  model {
>    alpha ~ multi_normal(gamma,
>                         diag_matrix(sigma_Sigma)
>                         * L_sigma
>                         * L_sigma'
>                         * diag_matrix(sigma_Sigma));
>
>
> (I just wrote the latter version this way for clarity --- quad_form_diag
> and multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose would be more efficient.)
>
> Ideally, to make this standard practice, we'd want a function
> with behavior defined by
>
>  vector ben_transform(vector mu,
>                       vector sigma,
>                       matrix L,
>                       matrix z) {
>    // validate sizes
>    return transpose(rep_matrix(mu,cols(z))
>                     + diag_pre_multiply(sigma, L) * z);
>
>  }
>
> But we could write it in C++ with the derivatives all done
> analytically.
>
> It's tempting, but I think not worthwhile to wrap the whole
> thing up with the priors on L and sigma.  For example, we've been
> working with models that place distinct informative priors on elements
> of sigma.
>
> - Bob

You can't use something from the generated quantities block in the transformed parameters block, in part because the stuff in generated quantities is executed after the sampling is finished. There are some functions in Stan that will automatically coerce integers to real numbers when appropriate, but it would not be appropriate in other circumstances, so there is no function for doing so.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Markian asked about converting integer to real, and
if that's the intent, then it's automatic.  Just like
in C++ or Java --- you can use an integer where you can
use a real.  For example:

  y ~ normal(0, 1);

the 0 and 1 are integers and normal takes (real,real) arguments.
You can also do this:

  real z;
  int n;
  n <- 3;
  z <- n;

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] missing data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] missing data
messages.body_plain:
As Dan notes there are some details in Chapter 7 of the manual, but I'll describe the general there here.

When dealing with missing data the general strategy is to build a missing-data likelihood for each pattern of missingness.  That way
you can partition your data into each different pattern and then your total likelihood is just

L_{complete} * L_{missing1} * … * L_{missing2}

In your case, for example, the natural patterns would be (1) complete, (2) missing just party choice, (3) missing just income, (4)
missing both.  The biggest problem with this strategy is actually computing the missing data likelihoods.

For example, let's say that our data is two-dimensional and the likelihood is modeled as a Gaussian:

p(x1, x2 | mu, sigma1, sigma2, rho) = Normal( x | mu, Sigma)

with x = (x1, x2), mu = (mu1, mu2), and Sigma = ( (sigma1, rho) (rho, sigma2 )).

In this case we can marginalize over x1 and x2 pretty easily to give the marginal likelihoods

p(x1 | mu, sigma) = \int dx2 Normal( x | mu, Sigma) = Normal( x1 | mu1, sigma1)

and

p(x2 | mu, sigma) = \int dx1 Normal (x | mu, Sigma) = Normal (x2, mu2, sigma2)

Then we'd have for each complete datum,

x_{complete} ~ Normal(x | mu, Sigma)

and for the missing data

x_{missing x2} ~ Normal(x1 | mu1, sigma1)
x_{missing x1} ~ Normal(x2 | mu2, sigma2)

Techniques like imputation essentially approximate these marginal likelihood distributions, but they tend to generate
inconsistent models that cause problems.  Others can speak more on this better than I.

That's all straightforward, if tricky to implement in practice because of the integrals needed to compute the missing
data likelihoods, but unfortunately it's not the end of the story.  The problem is that we've completely ignored the reason
why the data might be missing -- in particular, we're assuming that the data are missing at random and that the missingness
is not correlated with the value of the data.  But this is a bit suspect in survey modeling, especially with questions like
income!  Andrew discusses this in detail in "Bayesian Data Analysis", and ultimately the models become significantly
more complex (with effects like censoring).

It's probably easiest if you start with the complete data model that you'd like to fit and then iterate from there.  In particular,
first get it working in Stan (we're happy to help) and then with the full model in hand you can have the conversation about
missingness, censoring, and the like.

Good luck.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] "Bug" in MVN rng
messages.body_plain:
On Sep 24, 2014, at 3:25 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

> What's the problem with multi_normal_rng?
>
> Efficiency? I don't care always...
> Accuracy? I might care, given how bad the function performs.
>

Both.  We're moving to try to parameterize multivariates
in terms of their Cholesky factors rather than their covariance
or precision matrices.  It helps for both efficiency and arithmetic
stability.

> I suppose you suggest to use cholesky factors and sample standard normal variates instead, but then why shouldn't I let the multi_normal_rng do this work for me?

If you absolutely must have a covariance matrix parameterization,
then it's just a matter of efficiency whether you let multi_normal_rng
do the work or you do the work.  Doing it yourself, you can factor once
on the outside.  When we allow multi_normal_rng to return multiple
draws, then that motiviation would go away.

> I saw your tickets and I agree that having a function which outputs a vector would be very nice. In fact the function could figure out itself from the vector I have on the LHS how many random numbers I want, that would be really cool.

That's not possible.  Stan is purely compositional in that expressions
are evaluated only based on their sub-expressions, not based on the
context in which they occur.  I feel pretty strongly about maintaining
that property.  It's still compatible with conversions/promotions of
output (e.g., assigning an int to a real, which I really want to push
through cointainers everywhere if I can figure out how to do it).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the report.  That's definitely a bug in the
coding of that model for exactly the reason you state.

The bigger problem is that the model was too literally translated
from BUGS and it won't work in Stan as written (and we're not
convinced the BUGS models actually worked, either).  The problem
is with unidentified models as explained in the problematic posteriors
chapter of the manual.  It stems from Andrew's trick in his
book with Jennifer of using a parameterization
with an improper posterior and then trying to normalize the draws.
This won't work in Stan because Stan's too efficient at trying
to explore that improper posterior --- that is, Stan will let you
know you're trying to fit an improper posterior.   This is discussed
in the manual.

So we have to redo the example model so that it works.  We're
taking a pass through all the ARM models but hadn't gotten that
far yet.  Here's the issue to track:

https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/issues/5

We've done a fair bit of item-response modeling and
are going to be writing more as part of our IES grant.
Andrew wants us to change all the priors in all of these
models to be more informative and get rid of the uniform
vague priors on standard deviation.

I'm attaching a working item-response model and an R program
to simulate from it.  It's a little more complicated in that it
has hierarchical school-level effects.  And it still uses those
uniform priors on standard deviations (we'd probably now
use a cauchy(0,2.5) prior with only a lower=0 constraint).

- Bob

Does this mean that if there are 100, 1,000 or more CPUs in a cluster that Stan can leverage an "instance," i.e., a single CPU? If I'm none of these things and am little more than a hapless user who knows enough background IT to get some analysis done, am I basically screwed? Thomas,

Just a user here: Stan doesn't have parallellisation "inside", as
Michael said, so for parallel processing the approach is the simple
one of running multiple completely separate stan processes and
combining the outputs. See "Sampling in Parallel" in the cmdstan
manual (not the main stan manual, the cmdstan manual). They show
examples of running multiple processes, each with their own chain-id,
and a common random seed. This approach should be OK for
massively-parallel setups, though I haven't tried it. Stan works fine
on standard debian/ubuntu so I'd be surprised if you have to do any
difficult config on a cloud system such as amazon's.

Best
Dan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An IT Question: Running Stan on massively parallel platforms
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] An IT Question: Running Stan on massively parallel platforms
messages.body_plain:
Let me first say that there will not be one "answer", nor is there rarely such a concept when talking about clusters whose architectures can vary widely.
This kind of problem is not related to Stan but rather the architecture and administration of the problem at hand.

Firstly, at the moment Stan is single-threaded and entirely serial.  If you have multiple cores, whether they are cores on a single chip or cores in a large
cluster, then Stan can run on one and only one of them.  Just like any other serial process.

So if you want to run Stan with a billion data points within a single model then a cluster isn't going to help you (nor should it -- this is a deeper statistical
question that's best left for another thread).  But if you wanted to run multiple models or multiple chains, then a cluster might be of use.  In this case
the only question is whether or not the cluster meets the Stan dependencies.

If the cluster runs off a (presumably Linux-based) virtual machine then there's no problem.  You can configure the VM to grab Eigen and Boost and the
latest compiler and Stan will run locally in the VM without any issue.

If the cluster runs off a local environment then you have to ensure that he cluster admins install the necessary components for you (or give you the
permissions to do it yourself).  This can be easy or a pain, depending on how these kinds of requests are managed at a particular cluster.  But, again,
not something particular to Stan.

messages.body_plain:
We don't provide any out-of-the-box configurations for clusters
with Stan.  We've run Stan on clusters for experiments where we
want to deal with multiple parameterizatons, models, etc.  It requires
some basic cluster-specific config.

There's always an issue with configuring the local environments on
clusters.  Something like Amazon's EC2 lets you do that in a brute
force way by effectively taking a snapshot of an entire OS and then
running multiple instances of it.

Stan may be integrated into Shogun relatively soon (don't know what
their schedule or commitment level is), which may provide some hooks
to some clusters.

Given that you haven't said what problem you're trying to solve
and what hardware you have, it's impossible provide specific
suggestions.

- Bob

Hi,

First of all thanks for Stan, it really seems well engineered and extremely useful for continuous data. That said I'm having a few problems with count data. I want to model counts as some sum ove

messages.subject: Re: Noisy Poisson counts
messages.subject_clean: Noisy Poisson counts
messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

Stan should be fine for modeling count data, but like you say, doesn't allow integer parameters (HMC requires some transformation of the parameters to be continuous over the entire real plane). If you really really need integer parameters, the only solution is to marginalize over all possible values of the integer parameters by defining a mixture model (see the chapter on mixture models in the Stan manual). In some cases, you can marginalize things analytically, which may the case in your model.

>From your code it seems that you assume that the true counts and noise counts each follow independent Poisson distributions with rates counts.lambda[n] and noise.lambda, where the latter is hardcoded to 1. By definition, the sum of two independent Poisson variables X and Y again follows a Poisson distribution with rate (lambda_x + lambda_y), so in your case for each row n the rate is (counts.lambda[n] + noise.lambda). In other words, within each row, the sampling error in the data is still Poisson (i.e. variance equal to the mean), and you might just as well model the data as being Poisson-distributed with a parameter lambda[n] = counts.lambda[n] + noise.lambda, where the latter should also be defined as a continuous parameter.

In this particular example code, you assume to know the distribution of counts.lambda[n]. However, in your empirical dataset, this may not be true as you only observe the total counts (noise + true). If so, there is no way to identify what part is noise and what is true (lambda.noise could be anywhere between zero and the lowest overall rate in any of the n rows), and could just as well model the data as being Poisson-distributed with lambda[n] defined as a parameter, leaving counts.lambda[n] and noise.lambda unidentified.

Best,

Luc

If this is true, and I think you're saying this, Stan is not currently able to leverage the full distributed processing power in the cluster.   It would, however, be able to exploit the significantly greater (vs laptop) memory and storage capacity typically available in one of these environments.
> >

Could you provide guidance or be more specific about what this entails?  As we know, Stan is pretty much plug and play on laptops.  Do you have to be a Cloudera expert, a Hadoop manager, or a computer scientist to "configure the local environment" as you put it in an MPP to enable Stan to compile?  If I'm none of these things and am little more than a hapless user who knows enough background IT to get some analysis done, am I basically screwed?  Or, worse, would I have to pay a consultant hundreds, if not thousands of dollars to "configure the local environment?"

You're not really going to be able to use Stan to build
random forests.  It involves discrete non-parametric
components we can't sample over.

There's BART --- the Bayesian additive regression tree
package in R, but I don't know how possible it would be to
parallelize.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Noisy Poisson counts
messages.body_plain:
There's a description of how to do zero-inflated models and
hurdle models in the manual if you just literally need a 0-inflation
rather than a mixture of two Poissons or something.

The negative binomial is a gamma mixture of Poissons, and you
can often use the same trick to model the mean of a poisson as
a latent continuous parameter so you don't need to worry about
explicitly marginalizing out a discrete parameter.

- Bob

Also, I can see it is going to be inefficient to integrate out all the possible noise values. I think I might move to a mixture model. My counts appear to have a bimodal distribution with one mode close to 0.

Hello all,

To belatedly follow up on this conversation, I was eventually able to drive down the step size in my original application by setting "adapt_delta" very close to 1. This also reduced the proportion of divergent samples, though not quite to 0. The divergence problem reappeared as I ramped up the complexity of the model—I'm still working on trying to fix that. A possible factor contributing to the problem might be that the parameters of interest (all proportions) differ substantially in their magnitude, with some being very close to the boundary at 0. Might it be the case that the sampler is optimizing the step size with respect to the majority of proportions, which are not especially close to 0, and thus behaving poorly with respect to the minority very close to 0? Or is step size normalized to the scale of each proportion?

Devin

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob-
   Thanks for your observation.  The caveat is duly noted.  Dan's proposed a simple, brute force workaround that involves loading Stan across all of the available CPUs, running chains or ensembles of models, then rolling them all up at the end.  That's very practical and is in the spirit if not the letter of Cleveland's D&R approach.  Big data shops in the applied world are doing this, running millions of mini-models in a few hours on an MPP, then aggregating it all at the end to produce an approximate model.  I've also heard about a Bayesian vendor doing the same, generating billions of parameters in the process.  Brave new world it is.
Tom

messages.body_plain:
Step size is just a single value, but then there's also
a mass matrix that's estimated from the warmup sample covariance.
The default is a diagonal mass matrix with varying entries, but
you can insist on a unit matrix (forcing a single step size everywhere)
or use a dense mass matrix.

Numerical algorithms often run into problems when you get this kind
of poor conditioning --- matrix inversions with high ratios of highest
to lowest eigenvalue or stiff diff eq solvers (different dimensions evolving
at different time scales).  But Stan should be able to handle scales that
vary in dimension.

A bigger problem is usually that if you have something like a hierarchical
model, where the scale changes with the hierarchical parameter.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hey, sorry, I missed the replay with the metric components.

As Bob notes scales are set in two ways.  We estimate the marginal
variance of each parameter to set the diagonal element of the metric
(diagonal by default in Stan) and then we have an overall scaling
set by the step size of the integrator.

Now one immediate problem is the absolute size of your metric
components.  1e-6 is a tiny marginal variance, and may be running
into problems with our own adaptation algorithm which uses a
prior on the marginal variances of the order 1e-6 (that shrinks
with more warmup samples).  So some of those marginal
variances may be too big which is forces the step size to be
small to compensate and causing poor performance all around.

Marginal variances that small could also be an indication of really
large autocorrelations and way too little warmup.  In any case it
seems like the model may be too complex (folk theorem, etc).
Do you have hierarchical structure?  Are you using a non-centered
parameterization?

Another thing to look at is wether or not you’re saturating the
maximum three depth.  If so then NUTS is terminating early and
you’re not fully leveraging the power of HMC.  Saturation
is indicative of model problems and increasing the max depth
would only be a weak bandaid, but it may help.

When models start misbehaving this badly we can only speculate
without actually seeing code, unfortunately.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Bob and Michael. Your replies were very helpful. Regarding the code, it's actually fairly simple, so I have reproduced a version of it below:
data {
  int<lower=1> T; // number of time periods
  int<lower=1> N; // number of cells
  real<lower=1> priorN;
  real<lower=1> sampleN;
  real<lower=1> transitN;
  real Tgaps[T];
  simplex[N] props0;
  int<lower=0> countsT1M1[96];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[96, N] iotaT1M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT1M2[2];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[2, N] iotaT1M2;
  int<lower=0> countsT2M1[2];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[2, N] iotaT2M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT3M1[4];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[4, N] iotaT3M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT4M1[96];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[96, N] iotaT4M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT4M2[4];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[4, N] iotaT4M2;
  int<lower=0> countsT5M1[4];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[4, N] iotaT5M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT6M1[96];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[96, N] iotaT6M1;
  int<lower=0> countsT7M1[192];
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[192, N] iotaT7M1;
}
parameters {
  simplex[N] props[T]; // period-specific cell probabilities
}
model {

  for (t in 1:T) {

    if (t == 1) {
      props[t] ~ dirichlet(props0 * priorN);
    }
    if (t > 1) {
      props[t] ~ dirichlet(props[t - 1] * transitN / Tgaps[t]);
    }
  }
  countsT1M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT1M1 * props[1]);
  countsT1M2 ~ multinomial(iotaT1M2 * props[1]);
  countsT2M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT2M1 * props[2]);
  countsT3M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT3M1 * props[3]);
  countsT4M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT4M1 * props[4]);
  countsT4M2 ~ multinomial(iotaT4M2 * props[4]);
  countsT5M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT5M1 * props[5]);
  countsT6M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT6M1 * props[6]);
  countsT7M1 ~ multinomial(iotaT7M1 * props[7]);
}

The parameters of interest are the N-vectors of yearly proportions props[t]. In this example N = 192, but in other applications N can be as high as 10,000 or more. Obviously, as N increases the elements of props approach 0. If anything is unclear, please let me know.

Devin

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: NA and data organisation
messages.body_plain:
I think using magic number codings is confusing and also
fragile.

If possible, using the same kind of technique as for sparse
matrices may be clearer and less error prone and also tighter
in memory and runtime depending on the amount of missingness.

So if you have a vector y of size N, but it has some missingness,
then you create four arrays,

  y_obs[N_obs];
  idx_obs[N_obs];

  y_miss[N_miss];
  idx_miss[N_miss];

where the idea is that y[idx_miss[n]] = y_obs[n] and similarly
for y_miss.

I would recommend reading Michael's outline of the problem, too,
which I cut out and put into the next manual issue so I can include a version
in the manual:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/786#issuecomment-56707484

- Bob

On Sep 29, 2014, at 12:06 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Replacing the NAs with 99999 is the way to go but you then have to be very careful to never use a 99999 in a calculation. Basically, you need to declare in the parameters block a vector of unknowns whose length is equal to the number of NA values. Then in the model block make a hybrid observed data / unknown true data vector, that uses the data when it is observed and pulls from the vector of unknowns when the data is 99999. That hybrid can be used for a complete data likelihood and you should also model the probability that an observation is NA, presumably as a function of the hybrid observed data / unknown true data vector. However, this is all moot if you have missingness on discrete valued data because Stan does not permit you to declare discrete unknowns in the parameter block. Maybe just maybe you can do some data augmentation thing where you have continuous unknowns underlying discrete observables, but that is going to be tedious at best.
>
> Basically, Stan sucks at the sort of missing data problems that are commonplace in practice and this is the one area where the BUGS family of software has the biggest advantage over Stan. Although such models tend to be slow at best with BUGS and have at least as many problems with convergence, mixing, etc. as models for fully observed data.
>
> Ben
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for the simplification suggestion. With regard to multiplying the multinomial parameters, let me clarify. Each element of "props" is a vector of proportions corresponding to the cells created by a cross-tabulation of multiple demographic categories (e.g., FEMALE by BLACK by SOUTHERN). In most periods, the cell-specific counts are not observed. Instead, we observe marginal counts (e.g., countsT1M1) in lower-dimensional cross-classifications (e.g., FEMALE by BLACK). To sum the cell proportions into the coarser categories, the code premultiplies the props vector by an indicator matrix (e.g., iotaT1M1 * props[1]). This results in another simplex of proportions the same length as the count vector.

It occurs to me that maybe it would be better to first define the vector of multinomial parameters as a separate parameter (also a simplex), as in:
simplex[96] propsT1M1;
propsT1M1 <- iotaT1M1 * props[1]
countsT1M1 ~ multinomial(propsT1M1)
Would that help Stan handle the model better?

Sorry for not providing more information on the model earlier. I was trying to avoid overloading you with details.

Thanks for your help,
Devin

>   for (t in 2:T)
>     props[t] ~ dirichlet(props[t - 1] * transitN / Tgaps[t]);
>
> Too bad we don't have a vectorized version of multinomial yet, because

> > As Bob notes scales are set in two ways.  We estimate the marginal
> > variance of each parameter to set the diagonal element of the metric
> > (diagonal by default in Stan) and then we have an overall scaling
> > set by the step size of the integrator.
> >
> > Now one immediate problem is the absolute size of your metric
> > components.  1e-6 is a tiny marginal variance, and may be running
> > into problems with our own adaptation algorithm which uses a
> > prior on the marginal variances of the order 1e-6 (that shrinks
> > with more warmup samples).  So some of those marginal
> > variances may be too big which is forces the step size to be
> > small to compensate and causing poor performance all around.
> >
> > Marginal variances that small could also be an indication of really
> > large autocorrelations and way too little warmup.  In any case it
> > seems like the model may be too complex (folk theorem, etc).
> > Do you have hierarchical structure?  Are you using a non-centered
> > parameterization?
> >
> > Another thing to look at is wether or not you’re saturating the
> > maximum three depth.  If so then NUTS is terminating early and
> > you’re not fully leveraging the power of HMC.  Saturation
> > is indicative of model problems and increasing the max depth
> > would only be a weak bandaid, but it may help.
> >
> > When models start misbehaving this badly we can only speculate
> > without actually seeing code, unfortunately.

> >
> > > Step size is just a single value, but then there's also
> > > a mass matrix that's estimated from the warmup sample covariance.
> > > The default is a diagonal mass matrix with varying entries, but
> > > you can insist on a unit matrix (forcing a single step size everywhere)
> > > or use a dense mass matrix.

Each element of "props" is a vector of proportions corresponding to the cells created by a cross-tabulation of multiple demographic categories (e.g., FEMALE by BLACK by SOUTHERN). > countsT1M1 ~ multinomial(propsT1M1)

The computation's the same either way.

Not having an extensive background in applied computational stats,

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Missing data in matrix
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Missing data in matrix
messages.body_plain:
Just to clarify, I believe Bob and John are thinking about two different ways to hold out data for out-of-sample predictive validity (correct me if I'm wrong):

Bob: hold out a data point by putting it in a separate container in the data block and fit the model to the rest of the data; then evaluate the held-out data point in the generate quantities block.

John: just put all the data in a single container and negate the log probability of single data point (while also including it in the sampling statement for all the data) such that it effectively doesn't contribute to the posterior and the model is fitted to anything but that data point.

Bob's approach is cleaner and more efficient because it avoids unnecessary calculations. Further it avoids the risk of non-perfect negation due to differences in numerical stability between increment_log_prob() and sampling statements (if that is actually possible in Stan - probably not).

> I don't understand why there's a negation of the log probability
> for the "held out" data.
>
> If you really want to calculate the held out probability, you
> can do that in the generated quantities block, e.g.,
>
> generated quantities {
>   real heldout;
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     heldout <- heldout
>                + poisson_log(counts[n,heldout[n]], rates[heldout[n]]);
> }
>
> Then heldout should be the held out data's log probabilty in the model
> and there's no connection back to fitting.
>
> But you'll need to redefine rates in terms of the parameters, or
> move its definition into transformed parameters (but that will save it).
> The recomputation in generated quantities is relatively fast because
> there are no gradient calculations.
>
> This doesn't do anything like the "cut" in BUGS --- you still
> get connectivity in the model between the "held out" data and
> the estimates of rowrates and colsizes.
>
> It also looks like you have a multiplicative identifiability issue
> in that you can multiply colsizes by C and divide rowrates by C and
> get the same model.  The priors may be enough, but you should be careful
> with this.
>
> - Bob
>

John,

I don't know what platform you are using, but if you work in R (like me), pre-processing your data should be easy to automate. You would probably have to let go of your current matrix format and provide the data to the model along with two dummy integer arrays that identify the original positions in the matrix (if you absolutely need that). You can then do your outer product by looping through the data vector, using the dummy vector as indexes for your parameters. And then at the end, you only need one sampling statement, rather than N.

Dropping an item from the data vector (and the corresponding items from the integer arrays) during pre-processing of data should be no problem at all.

Luc

On Tuesday, 30 September 2014 08:06:58 UTC+2, John Reid wrote:
> Thanks Luc, that is indeed my intention although I certainly wasn't sure Bob's approach is more efficient. If the data is in a matrix format then I have to maintain indices into that matrix and dereference them for every data point held out or not. That appears to be quite some overhead to me and my limited benchmarks so far have confirmed this. The reason I asked the question was because it just was not working and I thought it should be a valid approach. That of course was due to a bug on my part.
>
> Thanks to both of you for your help,
> John.
>
>
> On 29/09/14 22:06, Luc Coffeng wrote:
> > Just to clarify, I believe Bob and John are thinking about two different ways to hold out data for out-of-sample predictive validity (correct me if I'm wrong):
> >
> > Bob: hold out a data point by putting it in a separate container in the data block and fit the model to the rest of the data; then evaluate the held-out data point in the generate quantities block.
> >
> > John: just put all the data in a single container and negate the log probability of single data point (while also including it in the sampling statement for all the data) such that it effectively doesn't contribute to the posterior and the model is fitted to anything but that data point.
> >
> > Bob's approach is cleaner and more efficient because it avoids unnecessary calculations. Further it avoids the risk of non-perfect negation due to differences in numerical stability between increment_log_prob() and sampling statements (if that is actually possible in Stan - probably not).
> >
> >
> >
> > > I don't understand why there's a negation of the log probability
> > > for the "held out" data.
> > >
> > > If you really want to calculate the held out probability, you
> > > can do that in the generated quantities block, e.g.,
> > >
> > > generated quantities {
> > >   real heldout;
> > >   for (n in 1:N)
> > >     heldout <- heldout
> > >                + poisson_log(counts[n,heldout[n]], rates[heldout[n]]);
> > > }
> > >
> > > Then heldout should be the held out data's log probabilty in the model
> > > and there's no connection back to fitting.
> > >
> > > But you'll need to redefine rates in terms of the parameters, or
> > > move its definition into transformed parameters (but that will save it).
> > > The recomputation in generated quantities is relatively fast because
> > > there are no gradient calculations.
> > >
> > > This doesn't do anything like the "cut" in BUGS --- you still
> > > get connectivity in the model between the "held out" data and
> > > the estimates of rowrates and colsizes.
> > >
> > > It also looks like you have a multiplicative identifiability issue
> > > in that you can multiply colsizes by C and divide rowrates by C and
> > > get the same model.  The priors may be enough, but you should be careful
> > > with this.
> > >
> > > - Bob

On Sep 30, 2014, at 12:24 PM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Isn't this the same as how an outer product works in the inner bowls of Stan? I guess it all boils down to that, as the efficiency gain from a fully vectorized sampling statement will be quite small as there are no shared components between the elements of counts (each is modeled by a different rate). Bob?

Correct.  I wouldn't expect to see much difference in performance from
vectorizing a Poisson that has a different rate for each count being modeled.
Vectorizing will eliminate a bunch of virtual function calls under the
hood, but in our measurements, those don't seem to take up much time (prefetch
seems pretty darn good when there's no branch prediction to go wrong).

But where you will save time is in not doing unnecessary log probability
calculations in the model that could be done in the generated
quantities block.  The reason is that we calculate gradients for everything
in the model and that's the main bottleneck in Stan's processing.
So anything to reduce the number of gradients or process them faster is
a win.  The generated quantities block just works on values (double in C++),
which are a lot faster to calculate.

- Bob

Basically, you need to declare in the parameters block a vector of unknowns whose length is equal to the number of NA values. Then in the model block make a hybrid observed data / unknown true data vector, that uses the data when it is observed and pulls from the vector of unknowns when the data is 99999. messages.subject: error tolerance for integrate_ode?
messages.subject_clean: error tolerance for integrate_ode?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

I don't have posting privileges on the developers group, so I am responding to a post from Sept 22 here. I am a regular user of numerical ODE solvers in the context of PKPD modeling.

> Right now, the error tolerance in the ODE solvers are set to
> 1e-6 absolute and 1e-6 relative.
> Question 1:  Why would we ever want an absolute tolerance?
>   Can I just make it the max double value?

That will be fine in cases where relative tolerance dominates, but it may lead to failures when absolute tolerance dominates, e.g., when the solution is near 0. By failure I mean inability to meet the tolerance specification with the specified limits on step size or number of steps.

> Question 2:  Can we just stick with 1e-6 relative tolerance, which is
>    what all the Boost examples use and pretty close to what everyone
>    seems to use for all these integrators across packages.  It seems
>    like 1e-6 is plenty of tolerance for stats, but I'm not an ODE
>    solving expert.

Relative tolerance = 1e-6 is probably a good default, but there will be occasions where a user will want to change it either to prevent integration failures or to increase precision.

> The error control is now for both the system itself and the
> sensitivities (derivatives of solutions w.r.t. parameters).
> Currently we have a single function w/o any user-specified tolerances:
>    integrate_ode(...);
> To allow control of both tolerances we'ed need three
> more functions since there's ambiguity in dropping
> arguments.  For example,
>    integrate_ode_tol(..., abs_tol, rel_tol)
>    integrate_ode_abstol(..., abs_tol)
>    integrate_ode_reltol(..., rel_tol)
> Question 3:  Do we need these?

I think it would be sufficient to have two functions: one with only the defaults and one that requires specification of all options. If an expert user really wants other choices, they can create them via user-defined functions.

> Question 4:  If so, can we put off adding the tolerances until later
>    or are these dealbreakers?

I'll take what I can get for now, but eventually want control of tolerances and possibly limits on step size or number of steps.

> If the answer to (3) is yes, we could use suggestions on how to test.
> Do we just set up some equations, set different tolerances, and check the
> ODEs determinstically?

For formal testing, deterministic tests using ODE's with known solutions seems reasonable. On the other hand when ODE solvers are exercised by sometimes extreme sets of parameter values within an MCMC run we learn more about what will break them. I encourage you to put prototypes in the hands of users who often require numerical ODE solvers and see what happens. I would be glad to participate.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the clarification on absolute/relative tolerances.
I think someone else wrote in recently and said the same thing.

There's no way to limit number of steps with the integrator
we're currently using (Boost's odeint).

We can eventually add in something to change tolerances, and it
makes sense to only have the fully specified version if both are
always relevant.

We're going to roll out our first version soon, which I think
will be more of a "prototype" than a finished product.  Maybe we'll
stick a "beta" sticker on it or something.

We're really bogged down in testing at the moment with four
different run conditions of known/unknown initial state and
needing to test all the gradients and error conditions (about four
different ways for each to raise errors).

We hope to have it done in another couple weeks, but who knows
what'll pop up next.  Right now, Daniel's wrestling with a bug in
make that's blocking all our testing.

- Bob
